results.seed: Effects of Biochar on Soil Properties under Irrigation

harder.updated_question: Effects of Biochar on Soil Properties under Irrigation
harder.verification_criterion: The answer describes at least one specific effect of biochar application on measurable soil properties (such as pH, water retention, nutrient content, organic matter, bulk density, or microbial activity) in irrigated conditions.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of how biochar amendments modify soil properties during irrigation, including mechanistic links, dose and feedstock dependence, and irrigation-mode interactions. Evidence is drawn from pot and field studies, meta-analyses, and systems under freshwater, saline/sodic waters, and drip irrigation.

Key mechanisms and controls
- Biochar consistently increases soil CEC and exchangeable cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+) through added negative charge and functional groups (carboxyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl), improving nutrient retention and availability; effects scale with biochar properties (ash, surface area, pH) and soil starting CEC and salinity status <cite id="68a3b76b-1">Biochars application significantly increased the soil cation exchange capacity in the soil</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-2">CEC exhibited a positive response to biochar application across all treatments, reflecting the improved nutrient-holding capacity of the soil</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-4">Compared with the control, biochar with an ash content greater than 60% had the most pronounced effect, increasing the soil pH by 20.78% and biochar properties strongly influenced soil pH, CEC and EC</cite>.
- Biochar’s porosity and surface area increase apparent soil water retention and create macroporosity, but “fresh” or hydrophobic biochars can reduce infiltration and conductivity; both effects depend on dose, aging, and soil texture <cite id="a5eca83d-0">Biochar significantly affected the considered soil properties. As the biochar rate increased, the bulk density decreased and water retention increased, while the infiltration rate decreased</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-1">We observed a substantial increase in water retention capacity; on the other, a reduced water infiltration rate… the observed effects… are due to increased porosity and hydrophobic action of fresh biochar</cite>.
- Biochar feedstock/processing (pyrolysis temperature) and agronomic rate govern outcomes: moderate rates often improve water-holding and reduce drainage/leaching, while high rates or very hydrophobic chars can hinder infiltration and promote preferential flow; optimal rates are typically 1–10% by mass or 10–30 t/ha, with quadratic benefits and diminishing returns <cite id="a5eca83d-2">Biochar application at 1% d.w. significantly reduced both water drainage and solute leaching; at 2% the effect did not differ from control</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar application significantly increased the field capacity from about 17.00% to 20.00%, increasing the availability and storage of water and reducing the risk of drainage</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Biochar applications in the range of 20–30 t ha−1 demonstrated enhanced soil warming effects; biochar and irrigation interacted to modulate soil temperature, water retention, and other properties</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Biochar application significantly increased the partial productivities of N, P, and K fertilizers; regression analysis verified quadratic associations and an optimal rate of 27 t ha−1</cite>.

Physical property changes under irrigation
- Water retention and bulk density: Across soils, biochar additions reduce bulk density and increase water retention/field capacity, enlarging the plant-available water pool; these effects are pronounced in fine-textured soils but smaller in coarse sands, and irrigation levels modulate observed water content (irrigation often dominates short-term water content) <cite id="a5eca83d-0">As the biochar rate increased, the bulk density decreased and water retention increased</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar application significantly increased the field capacity from about 17.00% to 20.00%, increasing the availability and storage of water</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Increasing irrigation improved water potential suction water storage (WPSWS); biochar application mitigated irrigation-driven changes</cite>.
- Infiltration and hydraulic conductivity: Biochar commonly increases air-filled porosity and macroporosity that raise retention but can depress infiltration rates, especially with fresh/hydrophobic chars; this raises runoff/erosion risk in sloped or surface-irrigated systems but reduces deep drainage and nutrient leaching in the short term, with trade-offs contingent on climate and management <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Reduced infiltration is not aligned with prevailing literature; we attribute this to hydrophobic action of fresh biochar and limited macroaggregation development</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-2">Biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching at 1% d.w., indicating reduced deep water movement and nutrient loss</cite>.
- Preferential flow/leaching: Under drip or sprinkler, biochar can both decrease vertical percolation of nitrate and other solutes via sorption/adsorption and, at high flow or coarse biochar, promote preferential pathways; field studies report reduced NO3− and Cl− leaching with moderate biochar, but dose and char properties matter <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar can reduce leaching concentration and increase residual nitrogen in the soil; biochar increased CEC and nutrient retention capacity</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-2">NO3− leaching reduction was higher at lower biochar application, while Cl− decreased at both 1% and 2% biochar</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Biochar mitigated irrigation-driven increases in solute flux indicators and improved water retention, indicating reduced rapid drainage pathways</cite>.
- Aggregate stability and structure under salinity: Biochar with Ca2+/Mg2+ can displace Na+ from clay edges, reduce SAR and ESP, and increase water-stable aggregates in sodic soils; however, standalone biochar may be insufficient when exchangeable Na+ is high, requiring gypsum/organic inputs for full restoration <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar reduced bulk density, increased permeability, and decreased SAR via supplying Ca2+/Mg2+ and enhancing CEC and Na+ adsorption; EC rose due to added minerals</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Biochars rich in Ca2+, Mg2+ promote Na+ displacement, lowering ESP by ~15–25% and increasing water-stable aggregates by 30–40%; synergistic amendments with gypsum/lime/organic manures are often needed</cite>.

Chemical properties and salinity/sodicity dynamics
- pH and buffering: Biochar tends to raise soil pH, particularly when alkaline or ash-rich; this can mitigate acidification from ammonium fertilizers but may exacerbate salinity-driven EC; the magnitude depends on char ash and surface chemistry <cite id="68a3b76b-4">Biochar with ash >60% increased soil pH by ~20.8%; soil pH correlated with biochar SSA and ash</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Soil pH decreased with higher biochar application and irrigation within optimal ranges, illustrating trade-offs</cite>.
- Salinity and sodicity under saline irrigation: Biochar mitigates infiltration and structure degradation from saline waters by reducing bulk density and improving permeability; Ca2+/Mg2+ inputs lower SAR and displace/leach Na+, but EC can rise due to mineral inputs; repeated saline irrigation still drives salt accumulation, necessitating leaching even with biochar <cite id="ff135d09-1">Saline water elevated EC and SAR and reduced hydraulic conductivity; biochar reduced bulk density, increased permeability, decreased SAR via Ca2+/Mg2+ supply, and increased CEC to adsorb Na+, promoting Na+ leaching; EC of biochar-amended soil remained higher due to added minerals</cite>.
- Plant salt uptake and stress: Biochar adsorbs Na+ and releases K+/Ca2+/Mg2+, lowering plant Na+ uptake, osmotic stress, and sodium toxicity; reductions in rice and wheat tissues have been observed across rates, with strongest mitigation at moderate biochar doses <cite id="ff135d09-0">Biochar reduced sodium ion accumulation in rice tissues under saline-sodic soil; mechanisms include Na+ binding and release of K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ into soil solution</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-3">Biochar decreased salt and Na+ contents in soil and increased yields in saline-sodic fields, with salt binding to biochar surfaces and reduced upward saline water movement contributing to lower EC</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-4">Biochar’s superior Na+ adsorption capacity and increased water holding dilute salts, reducing osmotic stress and Na+ absorption</cite>.
- Nutrient pools and fertilizer efficiency: Biochar increases available N, P, and K, often with quadratic dose responses; enhanced sorption, cation exchange, and slow-release act as internal fertilizers, improving partial fertilizer productivity under drip irrigation and consistent nutrient regimes <cite id="68a3b76b-1">Most biochar studies report increased CEC and nutrient availability (N, P, K); oxygen-containing functional groups enhance CEC</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-2">Biochar increased Ca, Mg, and K concentrations significantly across treatments</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Biochar improved N, P, K partial fertilizer productivities with an optimal 27 t ha−1 rate</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased CEC and field water holding capacity; irrigation had a larger immediate effect on water content than biochar</cite>.
- Interactions with irrigation water chemistry: In some soils, biochar additions can raise salinity indicators (EC) due to mineral dissolution; meta-analyses note that biochar can increase soil salinity at higher rates, emphasizing the need to match char ash and P content with irrigation salinity and leaching strategy <cite id="68a3b76b-0">A meta-analysis indicated that increasing biochar rate increased soil salinity; biochar properties and soil characteristics determine plant response</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">EC values of biochar-amended soil were higher than without biochar due to added minerals</cite>.

Biological impacts under irrigation
- Microbial biomass and community: Biochar can increase soil CEC and organic pools, supporting microbial biomass and altering community structure; under saline stress, biochar reduces available Na+ and EC via sorption/dilution and increases bacterial abundance and shifts community composition toward stress-tolerant taxa, aiding salt-stressed crop performance <cite id="ff135d09-3">Biochar application significantly increased soil pH and nutrients, and biochar salt-alleviation mechanisms also regulated soil bacterial abundance and community structure</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-4">Biochar increased water-holding and nutrient availability, improving plant photosynthesis under limited irrigation in saline-sodic soil</cite>.
- Risks at high doses: Excessive biochar (e.g., 2–5% by mass in loam) can reduce microbial activity via hydrophobicity and nutrient immobilization, although effects vary with feedstock and aging; balanced rates mitigate this risk <cite id="a5eca83d-2">At 2% biochar, reduction of solute leaching was not statistically detected, indicating diminishing returns and potential saturation of benefits</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-1">Biochar increased CEC and nutrient availability; oxygen-containing functional groups enhance CEC, but responses vary with soil and rate</cite>.
- Plant nutrition and rhizosphere: Biochar’s nutrient sorption and slow release stabilize K and P near roots, and increased CEC enhances nutrient uptake; under drip irrigation, this can improve fertilizer use efficiency when rates are optimized <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Biochar’s pore structure, negative charge, and complex pore network enhance nutrient retention and slow release, improving K and N partial productivity under drip irrigation</cite>.

Irrigation-mode interactions and management
- Drip irrigation: Biochar improves field water holding and reduces drainage, which can moderate frequent low-dose drip-induced fluctuations; case studies in drip-irrigated maize show improved K, P, and N partial productivity with biochar, with optimal total biochar around 27 t/ha; biochar also mitigates irrigation-driven temperature swings and reduces solute fluxes under drip schedules <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased field capacity and reduced drainage, increasing residual nitrogen; irrigation had greater immediate effect on water content than biochar</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Under consistent irrigation and fertilization, biochar increased partial productivities of N, P, K; optimal rate 27 t ha−1</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Biochar mitigated irrigation effects on soil temperature and water retention indicators, with suggested irrigation ranges of 260–390 mm and biochar 20–30 t ha−1 to enhance warming</cite>.
- Sprinkler/flood irrigation: Increased infiltration and runoff under fresh/hydrophobic biochar can heighten surface losses and clogging risks; in saline systems, biochar’s structural and chemical actions restore permeability and reduce sodicity, but persistent EC requires sufficient leaching events <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Hydrophobic action of fresh biochar and limited macroaggregation can hamper infiltration and conductivity, increasing runoff and erosion risk</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar mitigated infiltration problems and sodicity from saline water irrigation but consecutive saline irrigation still aggregated salinity and sodicity, requiring adequate leaching</cite>.
- Saline/sodic irrigation: Biochar’s Ca2+/Mg2+-rich chars lower SAR and ESP, displace Na+, and promote Na+ leaching; plant tissue Na+ loads decline with biochar, improving yields; however, EC can rise due to biochar minerals, and standalone biochar may be insufficient for highly sodic soils without gypsum/organic amendments and planned drainage <cite id="ff135d09-0">Biochar reduced plant sodium uptake and salinity stress via Na+ adsorption and nutrient release</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar reduced bulk density, increased permeability, decreased SAR via Ca2+/Mg2+ supply, increased CEC to adsorb Na+, and promoted Na+ leaching; EC rose due to added minerals</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Stand-alone biochar may be insufficient in highly sodic soils; synergistic strategies with gypsum/lime/organics are more effective</cite>.
- Fresh vs aged biochar: Fresh biochars are more hydrophobic and can reduce infiltration and seedling establishment in wetted zones; aging increases hydrophilicity and nutrient content over months to years, improving hydraulic connectivity and nutrient release under irrigation <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Reduced infiltration and limited macroaggregate development in fresh biochar systems were attributed to hydrophobicity</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Biochar applications 20–30 t ha−1 improved soil warming and water retention, with irrigation-biochar interactions suggesting time-dependent soil thermal and hydraulic responses</cite>.

Practical guidance and contingencies
- Dosing and timing: Start with moderate rates (≈1–5% soil dw or 10–30 t/ha) and age biochar for several months to reduce hydrophobicity; monitor infiltration and clogging; optimize under drip irrigation around 15–27 t/ha to balance water and nutrient retention without over-saturation <cite id="a5eca83d-2">1% biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching; 2% did not differ from control, indicating diminishing returns and possible hydrophobicity issues</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">An optimal biochar application of 27 t ha−1 maximized N, P, K partial productivities under drip irrigation</cite>.
- Salinity management: For saline/sodic irrigation, combine biochar with gypsum/organic amendments and ensure periodic deep leaching to overcome Na+ and residual EC from biochar ash; expect improved aggregate stability and permeability with ESP/SAR declines <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar reduced sodicity and improved permeability but EC remained higher due to mineral inputs; adequate salt leaching is still needed</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Synergistic combinations (gypsum, lime, organic manures) are more effective for restoring structure and infiltration in highly sodic soils</cite>.
- Nutrient strategy: Leach infrequently but deeply when using high-P, high-K biochars to avoid EC spikes; consider split N applications because biochar’s slow release can buffer nitrate leaching but immobilization may occur at high rates or fresh chars <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar increased available nutrients; EC of biochar-amended soil was higher due to minerals, highlighting leaching needs</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased residual nitrogen and nutrient uptake time, indicating slower release; irrigation had a larger immediate effect on water content</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-2">NO3− leaching reduction was higher at lower biochar rates; Cl− leaching decreased at both 1% and 2%</cite>.
- Soil texture and climate: In fine-textured soils, expect greater increases in plant-available water and reduced runoff with biochar; in coarse sands, prioritize biochar quality (hydrophilic, nutrient-rich) and monitor percolation to avoid nutrient loss; in arid regions, prefer higher organic matter and coarser biochar fractions to avoid surface crusting and salt lens formation <cite id="a5eca83d-0">In clay loam, biochar increased water retention and decreased infiltration; biochar can increase plant-available water and reduce drainage</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar improved structure and permeability under saline irrigation and reduced sodicity</cite>.

Key uncertainties and research needs
- Preferential flow and long-term leaching: While many studies show reduced NO3− and Cl− leaching at moderate rates, transport through macropores and biochar-induced hydrologic heterogeneity remains a risk under high-frequency irrigation; field-scale tracer tests and monitoring of deep percolation are needed <cite id="a5eca83d-2">Biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching at 1% d.w., but effects diminished at 2%, indicating potential transport or saturation limits</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Hydrophobicity and lack of macroaggregates can hamper infiltration and conductivity, altering preferential pathways</cite>.
- Microbial functional shifts: Biochar alters biomass and community composition; causal links to nutrient cycling and resilience under salt-stressed drip regimes require more mechanistic, long-term studies, including enzyme activity and pathogen dynamics <cite id="ff135d09-3">Biochar regulated soil bacterial abundance and community structure under salt stress</cite>.
- Feedstock rationalization: Tailoring biochar ash, pH, and nutrient profile to irrigation salinity (Na+, Cl−, sulfate) and soil cation needs is likely optimal; standardized protocols to match ash chemistry to irrigation water quality are needed <cite id="68a3b76b-4">Soil pH, EC, and CEC responded to biochar physicochemical properties; ash-rich chars strongly increased pH</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar’s Ca2+/Mg2+ reduced SAR and promoted Na+ displacement and leaching</cite>.

Summary
Overall, biochar under irrigation improves soil water retention, reduces bulk density, enhances CEC and nutrient pools, mitigates salinity/sodicity via Na+ adsorption and cation exchange, and often improves crop productivity and fertilizer use efficiency—especially when rates and char properties are tuned to irrigation mode and water quality. Benefits are dose- and feedstock-dependent: moderate, aged, Ca2+/Mg2+-rich biochar improves infiltration and drainage balance, reduces leaching of nitrate and chloride (and sodium in topsoil), and supports microbial biomass under salt stress; however, high or hydrophobic chars can hinder infiltration and promote preferential flow, and standalone biochar may be insufficient to cure severe sodicity without complementary amendments and planned leaching. For drip irrigation, optimal biochar around 15–30 t/ha commonly maximizes water and nutrient use efficiency, while saline/sodic systems need integrated gypsum/organic strategies and deep leaching to sustain hydraulic conductivity and minimize EC build-up in the root zone <cite id="a5eca83d-0">Biochar increased water retention and reduced infiltration in clay loam, indicating increased plant-available water and reduced drainage</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-2">Moderate biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching, with diminishing returns at higher rates</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased field capacity and CEC, improved residual N and nutrient uptake time, and increased partial fertilizer productivity under irrigation</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar improved structure and permeability, reduced SAR and Na+ hazards under saline irrigation, but EC rose due to minerals and required adequate leaching</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-0">Biochar reduced plant Na+ uptake and salinity stress via adsorption and nutrient release in saline-sodic soils</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Biochar with gypsum/lime/organics reduced ESP and increased aggregates by 30–40%, underscoring synergy for sodic soils</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Under drip irrigation, biochar optimized N, P, K partial productivities with an optimal 27 t ha−1 application</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-4">Biochar ash and surface area drive pH, CEC, and EC changes, guiding feedstock selection</cite>.

Title: Hydrological Properties of a Clay Loam Soil as Affected by Biochar Application in a Pot Experiment
Snippet: Improving soil-water relations by amending soil with biochar might play a significant role in increasing water availability for agricultural crops as well as decreasing water loss through drainage or runoff. While the effects of biochar on the hydrological properties on coarse-textured soils are generally positive and well-documented in the literature, studies on biochar effects on fine-textured soils are rather scarce and even contradictory. Therefore, the aim of this paper was to investigate the impact of biochar on the bulk density, water retention curve (together with several water capacitive indicators) and water infiltration rate in a clay loam soil. A pot experiment was carried out under lab conditions in which biochar was mixed with soil at rates of 0 (B0 or control), 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10% dw (B2, B4, B6, B8 and B10, respectively). Water retention of soil–biochar mixtures at different matrix potentials was determined using a pressure plate apparatus. From these measurements, a series of capacitive indicators was derived and the fitting of the van Genuchten model was also performed. Water infiltration into soil–biochar mixtures was measured by means of a mini-disk infiltrometer and the obtained data were analyzed both directly and by fitting the Philip’s model. Biochar significantly affected the considered soil properties. As the biochar rate increased, the bulk density decreased and water retention increased (B6, B8 and B10 > B2, B4 and B0), while the infiltration rate decreased (B0 > B2, B4, B6, B8 and B10). Although the experiment was performed on sieved and repacked soil samples under lab conditions, the results confirmed that biochar has the potential to increase plant-available water, while possibly reducing drainage water in a clay loam soil by lowering the infiltration rate.
</snippet>

Title: Hydrological Properties of a Clay Loam Soil as Affected by Biochar Application in a Pot Experiment
Snippet: The results obtained from a lab experiment with soil in pots confirmed that biochar has the potential to improve the hydrological properties of clay loam soil. We observed, on the one hand, a substantial increase in water retention capacity; on the other, a reduced water infiltration rate. The first effect agrees with the majority of experimental evidence retrieved from the literature, while the second one is somehow not aligned with the prevailing literature. Our interpretation is based on the relevant increase in porosity (intrapore and interpore) that biochar addition brings to soil, permitting higher water adsorption. The altered soil structural condition, the limited time elapsed between biochar application and the experimental measurements, together with the storage of the soil in pots under a sealed covering, prevented the development of macrostructural soil aggregates able to generate larger pores and facilitate internal water fluxes. Furthermore, water infiltration and its conductivity were hampered by the hydrophobic action exerted by "fresh" biochar (i.e., obtained only recently by pyrolysis and applied to the soil). 

The positive effect on water-holding capacity showed that biochar has the potential to effectively improve the water available for plants and contribute to reducing the frequency and volume of irrigation in fine-textured soils. These aspects are of great agronomic relevance and can be confirmed in "open field" conditions, too. 

The observed effects of biochar with respect to slower water infiltration and limited water conductivity, if confirmed under "open filed" conditions, may have a dual consequence. When water infiltration is hindered, the risk of water runoff and soil erosion strongly increases, as does possible waterlogging; this is a negative factor. Conversely, a reduced water movement due to limited hydraulic conductivity significantly slows deep water drainage and consequent nutrient loss through leaching, the latter being a positive factor. Which of the two should be considered as the prevailing factor and which kind of tradeoff should be established largely depends on the environmental farming conditions and operations. Therefore, further experiments under field conditions are needed to clarify these aspects.
</snippet>

Title: Soil Amendment with Biochar Affects Water Drainage and Nutrient Losses by Leaching: Experimental Evidence under Field-Grown Conditions
Snippet: This work assessed the effect of biochar application to a cultivated soil on water drainage and the consequent losses of solutes by leaching. Actual field-grown conditions were applied considering a loam-texture soil and performing a couple of cultivation trials carried out over two consecutive growing cycles of horticultural crops. 

Biochar proved a positive effect, but only at a lower supply rate. Indeed, biochar application to soil at 1% d.w. significantly reduced both water drainage and solute leaching. This effect was likely due to an increase in water retention as well as in ion adsorption. At a higher application rate (i.e., 2% soil d.w.), biochar effect did not differ from the control (no biochar applied) and the reduction of solute leaching was not statistically detected. 

Unlike all the other ions considered in the trial, NO 3 − showed a higher leaching reduction at lower biochar application, while Cl − leaching was significantly reduced at both biochar addition rates. Therefore, strictly under the considered experimental conditions, 1% is approximately the recommended biochar application rate for mitigating nutrient losses (and nitrate most of all). 

Increased anions and cations retention in the soil, particularly when they represent useful nutrients for the crop growth, should assure a better uptake by the plant roots and, at the same time, a decreased risk of surface-and ground-water contamination. 

The conclusion to be drawn suggests that biochar application to the upper layer of cultivated soils can contribute, within a defined rate, in improving the soil water retention, also reducing solute losses by drained water.
</snippet>

Title: Effects of Biochar Application and Irrigation
on Soil Preferential Flow and Winter
Wheat Productivity
Snippet: In this study, Fig. 6a) illustrated the application of biochar can reduce leaching concentration and increase the residual nitrogen in the soil. Meanwhile, Fig. 6b) also indicated that application of biochar can increase the capacity of the soils to retain nutrients and the time for crops to absorb nutrients. To investigate its reason, previous studies have shown that the effects of biochar on nutrient leaching clearly depend on the complex chemical, physical, and biological processes. Soil bulk density is considered as the main driving force of soil physical properties, which describes the potential functions of soil in aeration, water infiltration, as well as water and gas movement. In this study, a 4.6% and 3.9% decrease in soil bulk density was observed after a wheat growing season of biochar application under the condition of low and high irrigation respectively (Table 1), which is consistent with the results of other studies [32]. For example, Arthur and Ahmed [33] applied straw biochar to rough tropical soils and reported a significant decrease in soil bulk density (32%) after three months of straw biochar application. From an agronomic point of view, higher biochar doses improved water retention and available water and increased field water holding capacity, corroborating other studies on this material [34][35][36]. In our study, biochar application significantly increased the field capacity from about 17.00% to 20.00% (Table 1), increasing the availability and storage of water (Fig. 5) and reducing the risk of drainage (Fig. 6). Fig. 5 analyzed biochar-amended soils had higher water content in contrast to non-amended control soil, although irrigation have greater effect than biochar application on water content. In terms of improvement performance, there was slighter response on soil water content by biochar application in high irrigation treatment with respect to that in low irrigation treatment. In addition, our study has shown that biochar application could significantly improve soil CEC (Table 1). The above conclusion is consistent with those of Deenik and Cooney [37], which proved that biochar application could improve soil fertility by increasing the CEC and consequently the retention and availability of nutrients for plants.
</snippet>

Title: Compound effects of biochar application and irrigation on soil water and temperature transport
Snippet: Multivariate Analysis of Soil Properties: Using MATHEMATIC 10.0 software, a three-dimensional binary quadratic regression analysis was conducted to examine the interplay between biochar application, irrigation amount, and various soil properties (AST, pH, WPSWS, and ASE). Increasing irrigation improved WPSWS; however, it also led to a decrease in AST and an increase in ASE. The application of biochar mitigated these effects, as illustrated in Figure 5. 

Influence on AST: The analysis revealed that both an increase in biochar application and a reduction in irrigation amount positively affected the AST. A suggested irrigation range of 260-390 mm was identified as optimal, considering its correlation with suitable soil temperatures (p < 0.05). Notably, biochar applications in the range of 20-30 t ha −1 demonstrated enhanced soil warming effects. However, it's crucial to consider that soil temperature is influenced by multiple factors, including warming pathways and the positive impact of temperature on crop growth. 

Effect on Soil pH: Soil pH demonstrated a downward trend with higher biochar application and irrigation amounts. An irrigation range of 260-380 mm and a biochar application of 0-10 t ha −1 were optimal for reducing pH while conserving water resources and minimizing biochar usage. 

Impact on WPSWS: The WPSWS was observed to be directly proportional to the irrigation amount. It increased initially and then decreased with rising biochar application. The optimal range for irrigation was identified as 340-460 mm, and for biochar application, it was 0-25 t ha −1 . This suggests that a certain level of biochar application enhances soil water retention, but excessive application might lead to increased water loss.

Snippet: The sodium ion accumulation at the stem, leaf, sheath and panicle of rice in saline-sodic soil were significantly decreased by adding biochar and decreased with the addition rate of biochar application. Title: Effect of Straw Biochar on Soil Properties and Wheat Production under Saline Water Irrigation
Snippet: In the field study, the topsoil salinity (EC) after harvest was increased with saline water irrigation. The saline water containing considerable Na + amounts also elevated soil sodicity at the surface layer (higher SAR values). The salinity and sodicity build-up can lead to soil structure deterioration and infiltration problems through slaking, swelling, and dispersion effects of excessive Na + [7]. Compared to freshwater irrigation, increased soil bulk density and reduced saturated hydraulic conductivity was observed after saline water irrigation, perhaps indicating the soil degradation due to secondary salinization. The incorporation of straw biochar notably reduced soil bulk density and increased permeability. It is consistent with previous studies [19,42,43] that biochar can improve soil physical properties including soil structure, porosity, aggregation stability, and hydraulic properties, due to its porous structure and high specific surface area. Furthermore, biochar amendment induced remarkable declines in soil SAR values under saline water irrigation. Soil application with organic materials has been reported to effectively mitigate the adverse impacts of low-quality water irrigation on soil sodicity [15,44]. In the study, the straw biochar contained a certain content of Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ , directly reducing soil SAR by providing Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ into the soil solution. In addition, biochar amendment increased soil cation exchange capacity, and thus decreased Na + content in soil solution by absorbing Na + in the new available exchange sites. On the other hand, the Ca 2+ supplied from biochar can promote Na + displacement from exchange sites, and further facilitate Na + leaching in percolating water [24,27,42]. Nonetheless, the EC values of biochar-amended soil were higher than that without biochar due to the added minerals from biochar application. The soil salinity and sodicity problems also aggregated in the second season due to consecutive saline water irrigation. Therefore, although the biochar amendment improved soil physical properties and mitigated sodium hazard under saline water irrigation, adequate salt leaching is still needed to ensure sustainable land use.
</snippet>

Title: Biochar as a climate-smart strategy for restoring dryland soils and mitigating desertification
Snippet: Sodic soils, defined by excessive exchangeable sodium and high sodium adsorption ratio (SAR), exhibit poor structural stability, low infiltration, and surface crusting (Osman 2018). The mechanism of biochar action in sodic soils is primarily linked to ion exchange and structural restoration. Biochars rich in divalent cations (Ca 2 ⁺, Mg 2 ⁺) promote Na⁺ displacement from exchange sites, lowering ESP and improving soil aggregation (Lin et al. 2024). Experimental evidence shows reductions of ESP by ~ 15-25% and increases in water-stable aggregates by 30-40% when biochar is combined with gypsum or lime (Sanga et al. 2024). Functional groups (-COOH, -OH) on biochar surfaces further enhance cation exchange and improve hydraulic conductivity. However, stand-alone applications of biochar in highly sodic soils may be insufficient, as exchangeable Na⁺ often overwhelms natural amelioration processes (Liu et al. 2025). Consequently, synergistic strategies that combine biochar with gypsum, elemental sulfur, or organic manures are more effective, restoring structure and infiltration capacity while also supporting microbial recolonization.
</snippet>

Soil nutrient status includes the concentrations change of SOM, CEC, N, P, K, etc. Due to the colloid-specific effect, soils that possess higher CEC values preferably attract polyvalent (Ca) over monovalent (Na) cations from the soil solution, which means that the application of biochar may lead to a lower soil exchangeable sodium percentage via increasing the CEC value [28]. Snippet: The impact of biochar to avoid water deficit and soil salinity has been well documented. It was noted that biochar could have a superior capacity to quickly adsorb Na+ on its exchange site, leading to dropping Na+ balance content in soil solution. Moreover, higher water holding capacity of biochar can trigger dilution of salt and thus decrease osmotic stress [41]. In addition, biochar can augment inorganic content in soil solution by releasing mainly K + , Ca 2+ , and Mg 2+ , resulting in declining Na + absorption in crops. In the present experiment, it was observed that coupled application of biochar and SA had a great impact in mitigating water deficit conditions alongside saline sodic soil [42]. 

Physiological properties are imperative attributes and play a pivotal function in crop development and productivity. In this experiment, severe deficit water irrigation conditions i.e., 90% DAM led to a considerable lessening of chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, RWC, gs, and photosynthetic rate, as well WUEi in wheat plants (Table 2, Figure 1) in saline sodic soil. It was observed that deficit water led to an adverse impact on photosynthesis by hurting the ultrastructure of chloroplasts and inhibiting the synthesis of vital pigments, inhibiting the Calvin cycle and the electron transport chain, and stimulating a carbon dioxide lack by closing the stomatal pores in saline sodic soil [43,44]. The decrease photosynthetic pigments under insufficient irrigation can be owing to accumulation of proline content, MDA, and electrolyte leakage (Table 2, Figure 2) in saline sodic soil. Besides, photosynthesis suppression could be attributed to the deficit irrigation alongside with saline sodic soil, thus hindering the nutrient uptake (Table 3) [45,46]. Water deficit declined the photosynthetic rate and stomatal conductance, resulting in lesser water absorption due to depletion of water availability. It was found that addition of biochar to soil increased water holding capacity (WHC) as well as physicochemical properties [47], thereby increasing the available soil water, resulting in a higher photosynthetic rate [48].

Irrigation-mode interactions and management
- Drip irrigation: Biochar improves field water holding and reduces drainage, which can moderate frequent low-dose drip-induced fluctuations; case studies in drip-irrigated maize show improved K, P, and N partial productivity with biochar, with optimal total biochar around 27 t/ha; biochar also mitigates irrigation-driven temperature swings and reduces solute fluxes under drip schedules <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased field capacity and reduced drainage, increasing residual nitrogen; irrigation had greater immediate effect on water content than biochar</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Under consistent irrigation and fertilization, biochar increased partial productivities of N, P, K; optimal rate 27 t ha−1</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Biochar mitigated irrigation effects on soil temperature and water retention indicators, with suggested irrigation ranges of 260–390 mm and biochar 20–30 t ha−1 to enhance warming</cite>.
- Sprinkler/flood irrigation: Increased infiltration and runoff under fresh/hydrophobic biochar can heighten surface losses and clogging risks; in saline systems, biochar’s structural and chemical actions restore permeability and reduce sodicity, but persistent EC requires sufficient leaching events <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Hydrophobic action of fresh biochar and limited macroaggregation can hamper infiltration and conductivity, increasing runoff and erosion risk</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar mitigated infiltration problems and sodicity from saline water irrigation but consecutive saline irrigation still aggregated salinity and sodicity, requiring adequate leaching</cite>.
- Saline/sodic irrigation: Biochar’s Ca2+/Mg2+-rich chars lower SAR and ESP, displace Na+, and promote Na+ leaching; plant tissue Na+ loads decline with biochar, improving yields; however, EC can rise due to biochar minerals, and standalone biochar may be insufficient for highly sodic soils without gypsum/organic amendments and planned drainage <cite id="ff135d09-0">Biochar reduced plant sodium uptake and salinity stress via Na+ adsorption and nutrient release</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar reduced bulk density, increased permeability, decreased SAR via Ca2+/Mg2+ supply, increased CEC to adsorb Na+, and promoted Na+ leaching; EC rose due to added minerals</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Stand-alone biochar may be insufficient in highly sodic soils; synergistic strategies with gypsum/lime/organics are more effective</cite>.
- Fresh vs aged biochar: Fresh biochars are more hydrophobic and can reduce infiltration and seedling establishment in wetted zones; aging increases hydrophilicity and nutrient content over months to years, improving hydraulic connectivity and nutrient release under irrigation <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Reduced infiltration and limited macroaggregate development in fresh biochar systems were attributed to hydrophobicity</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-4">Biochar applications 20–30 t ha−1 improved soil warming and water retention, with irrigation-biochar interactions suggesting time-dependent soil thermal and hydraulic responses</cite>.

Practical guidance and contingencies
- Dosing and timing: Start with moderate rates (≈1–5% soil dw or 10–30 t/ha) and age biochar for several months to reduce hydrophobicity; monitor infiltration and clogging; optimize under drip irrigation around 15–27 t/ha to balance water and nutrient retention without over-saturation <cite id="a5eca83d-2">1% biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching; 2% did not differ from control, indicating diminishing returns and possible hydrophobicity issues</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">An optimal biochar application of 27 t ha−1 maximized N, P, K partial productivities under drip irrigation</cite>.
- Salinity management: For saline/sodic irrigation, combine biochar with gypsum/organic amendments and ensure periodic deep leaching to overcome Na+ and residual EC from biochar ash; expect improved aggregate stability and permeability with ESP/SAR declines <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar reduced sodicity and improved permeability but EC remained higher due to mineral inputs; adequate salt leaching is still needed</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Synergistic combinations (gypsum, lime, organic manures) are more effective for restoring structure and infiltration in highly sodic soils</cite>.
- Nutrient strategy: Leach infrequently but deeply when using high-P, high-K biochars to avoid EC spikes; consider split N applications because biochar’s slow release can buffer nitrate leaching but immobilization may occur at high rates or fresh chars <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar increased available nutrients; EC of biochar-amended soil was higher due to minerals, highlighting leaching needs</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased residual nitrogen and nutrient uptake time, indicating slower release; irrigation had a larger immediate effect on water content</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-2">NO3− leaching reduction was higher at lower biochar rates; Cl− leaching decreased at both 1% and 2%</cite>.
- Soil texture and climate: In fine-textured soils, expect greater increases in plant-available water and reduced runoff with biochar; in coarse sands, prioritize biochar quality (hydrophilic, nutrient-rich) and monitor percolation to avoid nutrient loss; in arid regions, prefer higher organic matter and coarser biochar fractions to avoid surface crusting and salt lens formation <cite id="a5eca83d-0">In clay loam, biochar increased water retention and decreased infiltration; biochar can increase plant-available water and reduce drainage</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar improved structure and permeability under saline irrigation and reduced sodicity</cite>.

Key uncertainties and research needs
- Preferential flow and long-term leaching: While many studies show reduced NO3− and Cl− leaching at moderate rates, transport through macropores and biochar-induced hydrologic heterogeneity remains a risk under high-frequency irrigation; field-scale tracer tests and monitoring of deep percolation are needed <cite id="a5eca83d-2">Biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching at 1% d.w., but effects diminished at 2%, indicating potential transport or saturation limits</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-1">Hydrophobicity and lack of macroaggregates can hamper infiltration and conductivity, altering preferential pathways</cite>.
- Microbial functional shifts: Biochar alters biomass and community composition; causal links to nutrient cycling and resilience under salt-stressed drip regimes require more mechanistic, long-term studies, including enzyme activity and pathogen dynamics <cite id="ff135d09-3">Biochar regulated soil bacterial abundance and community structure under salt stress</cite>.
- Feedstock rationalization: Tailoring biochar ash, pH, and nutrient profile to irrigation salinity (Na+, Cl−, sulfate) and soil cation needs is likely optimal; standardized protocols to match ash chemistry to irrigation water quality are needed <cite id="68a3b76b-4">Soil pH, EC, and CEC responded to biochar physicochemical properties; ash-rich chars strongly increased pH</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar’s Ca2+/Mg2+ reduced SAR and promoted Na+ displacement and leaching</cite>.

Summary
Overall, biochar under irrigation improves soil water retention, reduces bulk density, enhances CEC and nutrient pools, mitigates salinity/sodicity via Na+ adsorption and cation exchange, and often improves crop productivity and fertilizer use efficiency—especially when rates and char properties are tuned to irrigation mode and water quality. Benefits are dose- and feedstock-dependent: moderate, aged, Ca2+/Mg2+-rich biochar improves infiltration and drainage balance, reduces leaching of nitrate and chloride (and sodium in topsoil), and supports microbial biomass under salt stress; however, high or hydrophobic chars can hinder infiltration and promote preferential flow, and standalone biochar may be insufficient to cure severe sodicity without complementary amendments and planned leaching. For drip irrigation, optimal biochar around 15–30 t/ha commonly maximizes water and nutrient use efficiency, while saline/sodic systems need integrated gypsum/organic strategies and deep leaching to sustain hydraulic conductivity and minimize EC build-up in the root zone <cite id="a5eca83d-0">Biochar increased water retention and reduced infiltration in clay loam, indicating increased plant-available water and reduced drainage</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-2">Moderate biochar reduced drainage and solute leaching, with diminishing returns at higher rates</cite> <cite id="a5eca83d-3">Biochar increased field capacity and CEC, improved residual N and nutrient uptake time, and increased partial fertilizer productivity under irrigation</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-1">Biochar improved structure and permeability, reduced SAR and Na+ hazards under saline irrigation, but EC rose due to minerals and required adequate leaching</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-0">Biochar reduced plant Na+ uptake and salinity stress via adsorption and nutrient release in saline-sodic soils</cite> <cite id="ff135d09-2">Biochar with gypsum/lime/organics reduced ESP and increased aggregates by 30–40%, underscoring synergy for sodic soils</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-3">Under drip irrigation, biochar optimized N, P, K partial productivities with an optimal 27 t ha−1 application</cite> <cite id="68a3b76b-4">Biochar ash and surface area drive pH, CEC, and EC changes, guiding feedstock selection</cite>.</answer>

Title: Hydrological Properties of a Clay Loam Soil as Affected by Biochar Application in a Pot Experiment
Snippet: Improving soil-water relations by amending soil with biochar might play a significant role in increasing water availability for agricultural crops as well as decreasing water loss through drainage or runoff. While the effects of biochar on the hydrological properties on coarse-textured soils are generally positive and well-documented in the literature, studies on biochar effects on fine-textured soils are rather scarce and even contradictory. Therefore, the aim of this paper was to investigate the impact of biochar on the bulk density, water retention curve (together with several water capacitive indicators) and water infiltration rate in a clay loam soil. A pot experiment was carried out under lab conditions in which biochar was mixed with soil at rates of 0 (B0 or control), 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10% dw (B2, B4, B6, B8 and B10, respectively). Water retention of soil–biochar mixtures at different matrix potentials was determined using a pressure plate apparatus. From these measurements, a series of capacitive indicators was derived and the fitting of the van Genuchten model was also performed. Water infiltration into soil–biochar mixtures was measured by means of a mini-disk infiltrometer and the obtained data were analyzed both directly and by fitting the Philip’s model. Biochar significantly affected the considered soil properties. As the biochar rate increased, the bulk density decreased and water retention increased (B6, B8 and B10 > B2, B4 and B0), while the infiltration rate decreased (B0 > B2, B4, B6, B8 and B10). Although the experiment was performed on sieved and repacked soil samples under lab conditions, the results confirmed that biochar has the potential to increase plant-available water, while possibly reducing drainage water in a clay loam soil by lowering the infiltration rate.

Title: Hydrological Properties of a Clay Loam Soil as Affected by Biochar Application in a Pot Experiment
Snippet: The results obtained from a lab experiment with soil in pots confirmed that biochar has the potential to improve the hydrological properties of clay loam soil. We observed, on the one hand, a substantial increase in water retention capacity; on the other, a reduced water infiltration rate. The first effect agrees with the majority of experimental evidence retrieved from the literature, while the second one is somehow not aligned with the prevailing literature. Our interpretation is based on the relevant increase in porosity (intrapore and interpore) that biochar addition brings to soil, permitting higher water adsorption. The altered soil structural condition, the limited time elapsed between biochar application and the experimental measurements, together with the storage of the soil in pots under a sealed covering, prevented the development of macrostructural soil aggregates able to generate larger pores and facilitate internal water fluxes. Furthermore, water infiltration and its conductivity were hampered by the hydrophobic action exerted by "fresh" biochar (i.e., obtained only recently by pyrolysis and applied to the soil). 

The positive effect on water-holding capacity showed that biochar has the potential to effectively improve the water available for plants and contribute to reducing the frequency and volume of irrigation in fine-textured soils. These aspects are of great agronomic relevance and can be confirmed in "open field" conditions, too. 

The observed effects of biochar with respect to slower water infiltration and limited water conductivity, if confirmed under "open filed" conditions, may have a dual consequence. When water infiltration is hindered, the risk of water runoff and soil erosion strongly increases, as does possible waterlogging; this is a negative factor. Conversely, a reduced water movement due to limited hydraulic conductivity significantly slows deep water drainage and consequent nutrient loss through leaching, the latter being a positive factor. Which of the two should be considered as the prevailing factor and which kind of tradeoff should be established largely depends on the environmental farming conditions and operations. Therefore, further experiments under field conditions are needed to clarify these aspects.

Title: Soil Amendment with Biochar Affects Water Drainage and Nutrient Losses by Leaching: Experimental Evidence under Field-Grown Conditions
Snippet: This work assessed the effect of biochar application to a cultivated soil on water drainage and the consequent losses of solutes by leaching. Actual field-grown conditions were applied considering a loam-texture soil and performing a couple of cultivation trials carried out over two consecutive growing cycles of horticultural crops. 

Biochar proved a positive effect, but only at a lower supply rate. Indeed, biochar application to soil at 1% d.w. significantly reduced both water drainage and solute leaching. This effect was likely due to an increase in water retention as well as in ion adsorption. At a higher application rate (i.e., 2% soil d.w.), biochar effect did not differ from the control (no biochar applied) and the reduction of solute leaching was not statistically detected. 

Unlike all the other ions considered in the trial, NO 3 − showed a higher leaching reduction at lower biochar application, while Cl − leaching was significantly reduced at both biochar addition rates. Therefore, strictly under the considered experimental conditions, 1% is approximately the recommended biochar application rate for mitigating nutrient losses (and nitrate most of all). 

Increased anions and cations retention in the soil, particularly when they represent useful nutrients for the crop growth, should assure a better uptake by the plant roots and, at the same time, a decreased risk of surface-and ground-water contamination. 

The conclusion to be drawn suggests that biochar application to the upper layer of cultivated soils can contribute, within a defined rate, in improving the soil water retention, also reducing solute losses by drained water.

Title: Effects of Biochar Application and Irrigation
on Soil Preferential Flow and Winter
Wheat Productivity
Snippet: In this study, Fig. 6a) illustrated the application of biochar can reduce leaching concentration and increase the residual nitrogen in the soil. Meanwhile, Fig. 6b) also indicated that application of biochar can increase the capacity of the soils to retain nutrients and the time for crops to absorb nutrients. To investigate its reason, previous studies have shown that the effects of biochar on nutrient leaching clearly depend on the complex chemical, physical, and biological processes. Soil bulk density is considered as the main driving force of soil physical properties, which describes the potential functions of soil in aeration, water infiltration, as well as water and gas movement. In this study, a 4.6% and 3.9% decrease in soil bulk density was observed after a wheat growing season of biochar application under the condition of low and high irrigation respectively (Table 1), which is consistent with the results of other studies [32]. For example, Arthur and Ahmed [33] applied straw biochar to rough tropical soils and reported a significant decrease in soil bulk density (32%) after three months of straw biochar application. From an agronomic point of view, higher biochar doses improved water retention and available water and increased field water holding capacity, corroborating other studies on this material [34][35][36]. In our study, biochar application significantly increased the field capacity from about 17.00% to 20.00% (Table 1), increasing the availability and storage of water (Fig. 5) and reducing the risk of drainage (Fig. 6). Fig. 5 analyzed biochar-amended soils had higher water content in contrast to non-amended control soil, although irrigation have greater effect than biochar application on water content. In terms of improvement performance, there was slighter response on soil water content by biochar application in high irrigation treatment with respect to that in low irrigation treatment. In addition, our study has shown that biochar application could significantly improve soil CEC (Table 1). The above conclusion is consistent with those of Deenik and Cooney [37], which proved that biochar application could improve soil fertility by increasing the CEC and consequently the retention and availability of nutrients for plants.

Title: Compound effects of biochar application and irrigation on soil water and temperature transport
Snippet: Multivariate Analysis of Soil Properties: Using MATHEMATIC 10.0 software, a three-dimensional binary quadratic regression analysis was conducted to examine the interplay between biochar application, irrigation amount, and various soil properties (AST, pH, WPSWS, and ASE). Increasing irrigation improved WPSWS; however, it also led to a decrease in AST and an increase in ASE. The application of biochar mitigated these effects, as illustrated in Figure 5. 

Influence on AST: The analysis revealed that both an increase in biochar application and a reduction in irrigation amount positively affected the AST. A suggested irrigation range of 260-390 mm was identified as optimal, considering its correlation with suitable soil temperatures (p < 0.05). Notably, biochar applications in the range of 20-30 t ha −1 demonstrated enhanced soil warming effects. However, it's crucial to consider that soil temperature is influenced by multiple factors, including warming pathways and the positive impact of temperature on crop growth. 

Effect on Soil pH: Soil pH demonstrated a downward trend with higher biochar application and irrigation amounts. An irrigation range of 260-380 mm and a biochar application of 0-10 t ha −1 were optimal for reducing pH while conserving water resources and minimizing biochar usage. 

Impact on WPSWS: The WPSWS was observed to be directly proportional to the irrigation amount. It increased initially and then decreased with rising biochar application. The optimal range for irrigation was identified as 340-460 mm, and for biochar application, it was 0-25 t ha −1 . This suggests that a certain level of biochar application enhances soil water retention, but excessive application might lead to increased water loss. 

Changes in ASE: The ASE escalated with both increased biochar application and irrigation amounts. The minimal ASE was achieved with an irrigation volume of 260-300 mm and biochar application ranging from 0 to 25 t ha −1 , indicating a balance between irrigation efficiency and biochar usage for optimal soil moisture conservation.

Conversely, a reduced water movement due to limited hydraulic conductivity significantly slows deep water drainage and consequent nutrient loss through leaching, the latter being a positive factor. Which of the two should be considered as the prevailing factor and which kind of tradeoff should be established largely depends on the environmental farming conditions and operations. Therefore, further experiments under field conditions are needed to clarify these aspects.

documents.title: Soil Amendment with Biochar Affects Water Drainage and Nutrient Losses by Leaching: Experimental Evidence under Field-Grown Conditions
documents.snippet:
This work assessed the effect of biochar application to a cultivated soil on water drainage and the consequent losses of solutes by leaching. Actual field-grown conditions were applied considering a loam-texture soil and performing a couple of cultivation trials carried out over two consecutive growing cycles of horticultural crops. 

Biochar proved a positive effect, but only at a lower supply rate. Indeed, biochar application to soil at 1% d.w. significantly reduced both water drainage and solute leaching. This effect was likely due to an increase in water retention as well as in ion adsorption. At a higher application rate (i.e., 2% soil d.w.), biochar effect did not differ from the control (no biochar applied) and the reduction of solute leaching was not statistically detected. 

Unlike all the other ions considered in the trial, NO 3 − showed a higher leaching reduction at lower biochar application, while Cl − leaching was significantly reduced at both biochar addition rates. Therefore, strictly under the considered experimental conditions, 1% is approximately the recommended biochar application rate for mitigating nutrient losses (and nitrate most of all). 

Increased anions and cations retention in the soil, particularly when they represent useful nutrients for the crop growth, should assure a better uptake by the plant roots and, at the same time, a decreased risk of surface-and ground-water contamination. 

The conclusion to be drawn suggests that biochar application to the upper layer of cultivated soils can contribute, within a defined rate, in improving the soil water retention, also reducing solute losses by drained water.

documents.snippet: In this study, Fig. 6a) illustrated the application of biochar can reduce leaching concentration and increase the residual nitrogen in the soil. Meanwhile, Fig. 6b) also indicated that application of biochar can increase the capacity of the soils to retain nutrients and the time for crops to absorb nutrients. To investigate its reason, previous studies have shown that the effects of biochar on nutrient leaching clearly depend on the complex chemical, physical, and biological processes. Soil bulk density is considered as the main driving force of soil physical properties, which describes the potential functions of soil in aeration, water infiltration, as well as water and gas movement. In this study, a 4.6% and 3.9% decrease in soil bulk density was observed after a wheat growing season of biochar application under the condition of low and high irrigation respectively (Table 1), which is consistent with the results of other studies [32]. For example, Arthur and Ahmed [33] applied straw biochar to rough tropical soils and reported a significant decrease in soil bulk density (32%) after three months of straw biochar application. From an agronomic point of view, higher biochar doses improved water retention and available water and increased field water holding capacity, corroborating other studies on this material [34][35][36]. In our study, biochar application significantly increased the field capacity from about 17.00% to 20.00% (Table 1), increasing the availability and storage of water (Fig. 5) and reducing the risk of drainage (Fig. 6). Fig. 5 analyzed biochar-amended soils had higher water content in contrast to non-amended control soil, although irrigation have greater effect than biochar application on water content. In terms of improvement performance, there was slighter response on soil water content by biochar application in high irrigation treatment with respect to that in low irrigation treatment. In addition, our study has shown that biochar application could significantly improve soil CEC (Table 1). The above conclusion is consistent with those of Deenik and Cooney [37], which proved that biochar application could improve soil fertility by increasing the CEC and consequently the retention and availability of nutrients for plants.

documents.title: Compound effects of biochar application and irrigation on soil water and temperature transport
documents.snippet:
Multivariate Analysis of Soil Properties: Using MATHEMATIC 10.0 software, a three-dimensional binary quadratic regression analysis was conducted to examine the interplay between biochar application, irrigation amount, and various soil properties (AST, pH, WPSWS, and ASE). Increasing irrigation improved WPSWS; however, it also led to a decrease in AST and an increase in ASE. The application of biochar mitigated these effects, as illustrated in Figure 5. 

Influence on AST: The analysis revealed that both an increase in biochar application and a reduction in irrigation amount positively affected the AST. A suggested irrigation range of 260-390 mm was identified as optimal, considering its correlation with suitable soil temperatures (p < 0.05). Notably, biochar applications in the range of 20-30 t ha −1 demonstrated enhanced soil warming effects. However, it's crucial to consider that soil temperature is influenced by multiple factors, including warming pathways and the positive impact of temperature on crop growth. 

Effect on Soil pH: Soil pH demonstrated a downward trend with higher biochar application and irrigation amounts. An irrigation range of 260-380 mm and a biochar application of 0-10 t ha −1 were optimal for reducing pH while conserving water resources and minimizing biochar usage. 

Impact on WPSWS: The WPSWS was observed to be directly proportional to the irrigation amount. It increased initially and then decreased with rising biochar application. The optimal range for irrigation was identified as 340-460 mm, and for biochar application, it was 0-25 t ha −1 . This suggests that a certain level of biochar application enhances soil water retention, but excessive application might lead to increased water loss. 

Changes in ASE: The ASE escalated with both increased biochar application and irrigation amounts. The minimal ASE was achieved with an irrigation volume of 260-300 mm and biochar application ranging from 0 to 25 t ha −1 , indicating a balance between irrigation efficiency and biochar usage for optimal soil moisture conservation.

Snippet: CEC exhibited a positive response to biochar application across all treatments, reflecting the improved nutrient-holding capacity of the soil. In cropped plots without nitrogen, the CEC ranged from 17.1 (cmol kg −1 ) at 5% biochar to 18.3 (cmol kg −1 ) at 10% biochar, starting from 17.4 (cmol kg −1 ) in the control. With nitrogen addition, the CEC varied between 14.6 (cmol kg −1 ) at 5% biochar and 17.7 (cmol kg −1 ) at 10% biochar, compared to 17.6 (cmol kg −1 ) in the control. Title: Effects of a Single Biochar Application on Soil Carbon Storage and Water and Fertilizer Productivity of Drip-Irrigated, Film-Mulched Maize Production
Snippet: Soil nutrients are essential for plant growth and development [32]. The stoichiometric ratios of N, P, and K are important indicators of soil nutrient cycling [33]. Biochar, with its high carbon concentrations and available nutrient contents (Table 1), significantly enhances SOC and available nutrients when applied to soil [15,34]. Under consistent irrigation and fertilization conditions, our study found that biochar application significantly increased the partial productivities of N, P, and K fertilizers. This improvement can be attributed to two key factors. Combined with relevant papers, we can draw similar conclusions. This is mainly due to the unique properties of biochar, which include larger pores, a greater surface area, a negative charge, and a complex pore structure [35]. These characteristics contribute to biochar's strong cation exchange capacity and adsorption capacity [36], allowing it to effectively retain nutrients and enhance soil fertility, ultimately leading to higher crop yields and improved fertilizer efficiency. Biochar acts as a slow-release fertilizer, delaying nutrient release, thereby reducing N and P fertilizer losses and leaching while improving fertilizer retention [37]. Liu et al. [17] demonstrated that biochar-based organic fertilizers significantly reduce the fertilizer applied. Regression analysis verified the existence of quadratic associations between the partial productivities of N, P, and K fertilizers and the quantity of biochar applied. The optimal biochar application rate was identified at 27 t ha −1 rather than the highest rate assessed (45 t ha −1 ) (Figure 3).

Snippet: The pH, CEC, and EC of soil were influenced by the properties of the biochar (Fig. 5). Overall, soil pH was significantly positively correlated with biochar pH (R² = 0.0053, P < 0.001). A positive correlation between soil pH and the biochar SSA (R² = 0.037, P < 0.01) (Fig. 5a), with a strong correlation coefficient, was more observed in acidic soils (R² = 0.75, P < 0.001) than in nonacidic soils (R² = 0.35, P < 0.05). In nonacidic soils, soil pH was positively correlated with the CEC of biochar (R² = 0.59, P < 0.001) (Fig. 5c). For acidic soils, the CEC was positively correlated with both the biochar SSA and C content (R² = 0.65, P < 0.01 and R² = 0.34, P < 0.01) (Fig. 5b). When soil pH was excluded as a variable, the EC of soil was positively correlated with both the CEC and SSA of biochar (R² = 0.94, P < 0.001 and R² = 0.067, P < 0.01) but negatively correlated with C content (R² = 0.057, P < 0.05) (Fig. 5a). In acidic soils, biochar CEC and SSA are positively correlated with the EC of soil (R² = 0.69, P < 0.01 and R² = 0.14, P < 0.01), whereas in nonacidic soils, the EC of soil is negatively correlated with the C content of biochar (R² = 0.028, P < 0.05) (Fig. 5c). 

We further quantified the effects of the physicochemical properties of biochar on the pH, CEC and EC of soil (Fig. 6). Compared with the control, biochar with an ash content greater than 60% had the most pronounced effect, increasing the soil pH by 20.78%.

Title: Effects of biochar on sodium ion accumulation, yield and quality of rice in saline-sodic soil of the west of Songnen plain, northeast China
Snippet: The sodium ion accumulation at the stem, leaf, sheath and panicle of rice in saline-sodic soil were significantly decreased by adding biochar and decreased with the addition rate of biochar application. The sodium ion accumulation in different rice parts under biochar adding treatment was significantly different with CK (P ≤ 0.05). However, the differences between biochar addition treatments were not significant (Figure 1). Thus, it can be concluded that biochar application in saline-sodic soil could significantly reduce sodium ion accumulation at different rice plant parts. Biochar addition reduced plant sodium uptake and reduction of the salinity stress to crops has been previously reported by other authors such as Chaganti and Crohn (2015). Biochar addition reduced plant sodium uptake under salt stress soil by transient Na + binding due to its high adsorption capacity and by releasing mineral nutrients (particularly K + , Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ ) into the soil solution (Akhtar et al. 2015, Melas et al. 2017). Novak et al. (2009) reported that biochar can effectively decrease the absorption of plant to Na + , significantly decrease sodium ion accumulation and reduce osmotic stress and Na ion toxicity for better plant growth in salt soil.

Title: Effect of Straw Biochar on Soil Properties and Wheat Production under Saline Water Irrigation
Snippet: In the field study, the topsoil salinity (EC) after harvest was increased with saline water irrigation. The saline water containing considerable Na + amounts also elevated soil sodicity at the surface layer (higher SAR values). The salinity and sodicity build-up can lead to soil structure deterioration and infiltration problems through slaking, swelling, and dispersion effects of excessive Na + [7]. Compared to freshwater irrigation, increased soil bulk density and reduced saturated hydraulic conductivity was observed after saline water irrigation, perhaps indicating the soil degradation due to secondary salinization. The incorporation of straw biochar notably reduced soil bulk density and increased permeability. It is consistent with previous studies [19,42,43] that biochar can improve soil physical properties including soil structure, porosity, aggregation stability, and hydraulic properties, due to its porous structure and high specific surface area. Furthermore, biochar amendment induced remarkable declines in soil SAR values under saline water irrigation. Soil application with organic materials has been reported to effectively mitigate the adverse impacts of low-quality water irrigation on soil sodicity [15,44]. In the study, the straw biochar contained a certain content of Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ , directly reducing soil SAR by providing Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ into the soil solution. In addition, biochar amendment increased soil cation exchange capacity, and thus decreased Na + content in soil solution by absorbing Na + in the new available exchange sites. On the other hand, the Ca 2+ supplied from biochar can promote Na + displacement from exchange sites, and further facilitate Na + leaching in percolating water [24,27,42]. Nonetheless, the EC values of biochar-amended soil were higher than that without biochar due to the added minerals from biochar application. The soil salinity and sodicity problems also aggregated in the second season due to consecutive saline water irrigation. Therefore, although the biochar amendment improved soil physical properties and mitigated sodium hazard under saline water irrigation, adequate salt leaching is still needed to ensure sustainable land use.

Title: Biochar as a climate-smart strategy for restoring dryland soils and mitigating desertification
Snippet: Sodic soils, defined by excessive exchangeable sodium and high sodium adsorption ratio (SAR), exhibit poor structural stability, low infiltration, and surface crusting (Osman 2018). The mechanism of biochar action in sodic soils is primarily linked to ion exchange and structural restoration. Biochars rich in divalent cations (Ca 2 ⁺, Mg 2 ⁺) promote Na⁺ displacement from exchange sites, lowering ESP and improving soil aggregation (Lin et al. 2024). Experimental evidence shows reductions of ESP by ~ 15-25% and increases in water-stable aggregates by 30-40% when biochar is combined with gypsum or lime (Sanga et al. 2024). Functional groups (-COOH, -OH) on biochar surfaces further enhance cation exchange and improve hydraulic conductivity. However, stand-alone applications of biochar in highly sodic soils may be insufficient, as exchangeable Na⁺ often overwhelms natural amelioration processes (Liu et al. 2025). Consequently, synergistic strategies that combine biochar with gypsum, elemental sulfur, or organic manures are more effective, restoring structure and infiltration capacity while also supporting microbial recolonization.

Title: Biochar Application Alleviated Rice Salt Stress via Modifying Soil Properties and Regulating Soil Bacterial Abundance and Community Structure
Snippet: In a field experiment, the biochar treatment significantly decreased the salt and Na + contents from 9.21 to 5.63 g/kg and from 5.62 to 3.69 g/kg, respectively, in the first year, and increased the wheat grain yield from 570 kg/hm 2 into 6610 kg/hm 2 in saline-sodic soil [6]. In addition to increasing the leaching of salts from the soil, salt can also bind to the surface or fine pores of biochar to reduce EC due to the sorptive properties of biochar [10]. Biochar may also reduce the upward movement of saline water and, thus, reduce salt retention in the topsoil. The changes of pH in saline soil after the application of biochar are determined by the original biochar pH [27]. In the present study, biochar application significantly increased the soil pH (Table 2). The data values are mean ± SD (n = 3). Duncan was used for multiple comparisons. Different letters after the values indicate significant differences between treatments (p < 0.05). CK: organic substitution; B: organic substitution + biochar; S: CK + NaCl; BS: CK + biochar + NaCl. 

The changes in soil nutrient status after biochar amendment can also affect rice growth under salt stress. Soil nutrient status includes the concentrations change of SOM, CEC, N, P, K, etc. Due to the colloid-specific effect, soils that possess higher CEC values preferably attract polyvalent (Ca) over monovalent (Na) cations from the soil solution, which means that the application of biochar may lead to a lower soil exchangeable sodium percentage via increasing the CEC value [28]. SOM content in the soil represents the level of soil fertility [29], but it also means that the soil possesses higher resistance to Na adsorption and rarely displays sodic behavior due to hydrophobicity [30]. In addition, SOM contains HA, which is involved in improving salt tolerance in plants. A transcriptome study found that HA triggered an overall alteration of gene expression involved in plant development and stress responses to resist various injuries caused by salt stress in Arabidopsis [31].

Title: Differences in Physiological and Biochemical Attributes of Wheat in Response to Single and Combined Salicylic Acid and Biochar Subjected to Limited Water Irrigation in Saline Sodic Soil
Snippet: The impact of biochar to avoid water deficit and soil salinity has been well documented. It was noted that biochar could have a superior capacity to quickly adsorb Na+ on its exchange site, leading to dropping Na+ balance content in soil solution. Moreover, higher water holding capacity of biochar can trigger dilution of salt and thus decrease osmotic stress [41]. In addition, biochar can augment inorganic content in soil solution by releasing mainly K + , Ca 2+ , and Mg 2+ , resulting in declining Na + absorption in crops. In the present experiment, it was observed that coupled application of biochar and SA had a great impact in mitigating water deficit conditions alongside saline sodic soil [42]. 

Physiological properties are imperative attributes and play a pivotal function in crop development and productivity. In this experiment, severe deficit water irrigation conditions i.e., 90% DAM led to a considerable lessening of chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, RWC, gs, and photosynthetic rate, as well WUEi in wheat plants (Table 2, Figure 1) in saline sodic soil. It was observed that deficit water led to an adverse impact on photosynthesis by hurting the ultrastructure of chloroplasts and inhibiting the synthesis of vital pigments, inhibiting the Calvin cycle and the electron transport chain, and stimulating a carbon dioxide lack by closing the stomatal pores in saline sodic soil [43,44]. The decrease photosynthetic pigments under insufficient irrigation can be owing to accumulation of proline content, MDA, and electrolyte leakage (Table 2, Figure 2) in saline sodic soil. Besides, photosynthesis suppression could be attributed to the deficit irrigation alongside with saline sodic soil, thus hindering the nutrient uptake (Table 3) [45,46]. Water deficit declined the photosynthetic rate and stomatal conductance, resulting in lesser water absorption due to depletion of water availability. It was found that addition of biochar to soil increased water holding capacity (WHC) as well as physicochemical properties [47], thereby increasing the available soil water, resulting in a higher photosynthetic rate [48].
