judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer explicitly addresses whether water retention benefits persist or degrade over multi-year irrigation timeframes by citing longitudinal field evidence. It presents: (1) a 6-year field aging study [5] showing changes in water-absorbing capacity and soil water retention capacity; (2) field trials showing biochar raised wilting point and delayed wilting across irrigation cycles [3]; (3) multi-season evidence from subsurface drip irrigation systems [4]; and (4) a 1-71 year chronosequence [1] showing decadal-scale structural evolution with pore frameworks retained but with accumulating coatings/fillings. The answer also describes the trajectory (initial gains followed by gradual attenuation due to pore occlusion over years to decades) and acknowledges that 'most field trials are 1-3 years, leaving decadal durability under continuous irrigation underreported.' This satisfies both pathways of the criterion: it cites multi-year field data AND acknowledges gaps in long-term empirical evidence.
other_issues: The answer could be more concise - it includes extensive detail about mechanisms and management recommendations that, while valuable, make it harder to extract the core findings about long-term persistence.

Reference [3] studies Ehretia asperula (a woody plant) under withholding irrigation experiments, not repeated irrigation cycles over multiple years in a crop production system - this is somewhat tangential to the question's focus on 'multi-year irrigation cycles.'

The chronosequence study [1] examines pyrogenic char from forest fires in boreal forest soil, not agricultural biochar under irrigation - while informative about aging mechanisms, the relevance to irrigated agricultural systems is indirect.

Minor: The answer states biochar can 'increase hygroscopic water uptake' due to 'hydrophobic surfaces' - this is contradictory since hydrophobic surfaces repel water and would not enhance hygroscopic uptake. The mechanism description appears confused between hydrophobic/hydrophilic properties.

However, some cited studies have limited direct relevance to the specific question (forest pyrogenic char, woody ornamental plants), and there is a conceptual error conflating hydrophobic and hygroscopic properties.

Summary and framing under irrigation
Biochar commonly improves irrigation-relevant soil functions by increasing porosity and water retention in coarse-textured soils, enhancing cation and nutrient sorption, and modulating pH and electrical conductivity (EC) via its ash and functional groups; however, these same properties can turn disadvantages if applied in excess, triggering nutrient immobilization during early decomposition, surface alkalinity/efflorescence, or waterlogging/anaerobiosis, especially in sands under frequent leaching and in clays where buffering and drainage constraints are different. <cite id="fde4ec35-0">In sandy soils, biochar’s porous structure increases water retention, CEC, and nutrient sorption, reducing leaching and improving nutrient use efficiency</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-3">and irrigation studies report that dose-dependent increases in pH and EC arise from carbonate dissolution and cation release from biochar, with leaching shifting salts deeper and altering infiltration</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-0">By contrast, in fine-textured soils biochar’s fixed pore sizes decrease moisture availability and can raise bulk density, whereas nutrient retention improvements can still reduce nutrient leaching</cite>.

Sandy soils: when peak improvements occur and why
Across irrigated sandy systems, multiple lines of evidence converge on modest to moderate biochar rates delivering peak gains in water retention, infiltration, and nutrient retention, with deterioration when rates are high due to immobilization and/or surface alkalinity. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">In a coastal saline sandy soil, 1% biochar reduced exchangeable sodium (Na) and salt stress relative to untreated controls, while a higher 2% dose did not further reduce salinity under 10 PSU conditions; nutrient pools increased (K up ~35–68%, Ca up to ~0.44%), and pH rose with dose, illustrating that biochar bound K and Ca and raised alkalinity potential</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-1">Under sandy loam in varied irrigation regimes, increasing biochar dose generally increased available P and K, with higher-dose biochar richer in available P particularly beneficial where background P was low</cite>. <cite id="fde4ec35-1">For turfgrass grown on sandy Ultisols, an optimal incorporation near 10% v/v improved water/nutrient retention and root performance, but more than 10% detrimentally affected root depth due to anaerobic conditions from higher water retention</cite>. <cite id="fde4ec35-4">In alkaline, coarse-textured soils, biochar decreased nitrate leaching and increased mineral N at harvest, highlighting that biochar’s chemistry enhances N retention and long-term availability</cite>.

Mechanistically, the “sweet spot” in sands under irrigation reflects a balance between added porosity/CEC (which cut leaching), immediate nutrient immobilization during biochar decomposition (due to C:N), and risk of surface alkalinity and salt efflorescence from Ca and carbonate-bearing feedstocks. <cite id="fde4ec35-0">Biochar adsorbs cations and increases CEC in sandy soils, reducing nutrient leaching</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-3">but higher doses raise pH and EC via dissolution of biochar surface carbonates and cation exchange, creating conditions favorable to Na/CO3 efflorescence and potential phytotoxic alkalinity</cite>. <cite id="64948a1f-2">Synthesis across stress studies indicates yield responses often rise to moderate biochar rates (2–5% by weight) and then level or decline, with higher doses risking nutrient immobilization</cite>.

Practical implication: for sandy soils under irrigation, peak improvements in infiltration, water retention, P/K availability, and yield tend to occur around 1–2% w/w biochar in most settings, with higher “volume” rates near 10% v/v effective for rooting but risking waterlogging above ~10% v/v; exceeding ~2–3% w/w with alkaline/ashy biochars can elevate surface alkalinity and trigger Ca/Na efflorescences, especially under low leaching fractions. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">One coastal sandy study achieved salinity mitigation at 1% biochar and showed diminishing returns at 2% for salinity reduction, while nutrient sorption and pH kept rising with dose</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-1">and turfgrass work suggests ~10% v/v is a root/WHC tipping point in sandy Ultisols</cite> <cite id="64948a1f-2">with 2–5% often peaking nutrient availability before immobilization risk increases</cite>.

Clay soils: when peak improvements occur and why
In fine-textured/clay soils, biochar also improves aggregation, porosity, and nutrient sorption, but the soil’s inherent drainage constraints and buffering mean problems can arise at higher rates via surface sealing, reduced macroporosity, and alkalinity-driven nutrient lock-up. <cite id="b68d0bac-0">Biochar increases macroaggregation and modifies hydraulic properties; in clays it can reduce available moisture relative to sands due to packing effects</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-2">Under wastewater irrigation (high EC inflows), higher biochar rates more strongly increased EC and nutrients by boosting cation/anion release and adsorption, indicating that nutrient-binding capacity can raise salinity indices for clays</cite>. Critically, dose–response mapping in tropical fine-textured soils shows that while low rates improve fertility, higher rates can overshoot optimal pH and deplete available P/NH4, with some optimal performance at ~2% w/w in Vertisols/Ferralsols before penalties emerge. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">A 2% application rate was optimal in Acrisol, Red Ferralsol, and Vertisol; rates >0.25–0.3% raised pH above 7 in Ferralsols and decreased TOC, available P, and NH4+, whereas 2% restored NO3− and improved maize biomass and root elongation, underscoring strong clay-type dependence</cite>.

Mechanistically, clays peak at higher initial rates before alkalinity and nutrient sorption/immobilization trade-offs dominate because their high buffering power and CEC retain more cations, but biochar’s ash and functional groups can push pH into alkaline ranges, precipitating Ca–Corg complexes and phosphates and reducing NH4+ availability until rainfall/leaching mobilizes residues. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">In Red Ferralsols, rates above 0.25% increased pH beyond 7, with concomitant drops in TOC, available P, and NH4+, while 2% biochar increased NO3− and improved root growth and yield, indicating a non-monotonic response where early immobilization occurs before later nutrient release and structure benefits dominate</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-2">Higher rates under wastewater irrigation further raise EC and nutrient adsorption/desorption, which can stress salinity-sensitive crops on clays</cite>. Meta-analyses also caution that alkaline/fine-textured soils benefit less from biochar, and high rates are best reserved for single, strategic applications to reach thresholds, rather than repeated annual dosing. <cite id="64948a1f-4">Meta-analyses show strongly acidic, coarse-textured soils respond more than neutral/alkaline, fine-textured soils; biochar at >10 Mg ha−1 enhances P availability in pH<7.5 soils but has little effect in alkaline soils, supporting a one-off or lower-frequency dosing strategy</cite>.

Putting numbers together: peak ranges and transition to harm under irrigation
- Sands (Ultisols/coastal/plains): A pragmatic dose–response pattern under irrigation shows improvements in WHC, infiltration, P/K availability, and yield peak at roughly 1–2% biochar (w/w), with evidence of diminishing or reversing returns when exceeding ~2–3% w/w—especially for alkaline/ashy biochars where surface alkalinity and efflorescence risk rise. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">In coastal saline sands, 1% biochar lowered Na and salt stress, while 2% did not further reduce salinity; pH and EC rose with dose due to carbonate/cation release</cite>. <cite id="fde4ec35-1">For turfgrass, about 10% v/v improved WHC and rooting, but >10% v/v reduced root depth by promoting anaerobiosis</cite>. <cite id="64948a1f-2">Across stress conditions, moderate rates of 2–5% by weight commonly peak nutrient availability and yield before immobilization sets in</cite>. Under sprinkler/flood irrigation with low leaching fractions, holding to ≤1–2% w/w of wood-derived, lower-lime biochar is safer to avoid alkalinity and nutrient lock-up; sands with good leaching (e.g., drip with 10–30% leaching fractions) can tolerate up to ~3–5% w/w for structural/CEC benefits if monitored for EC/P availability and early nutrient immobilization. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Dose-dependent EC and pH shifts illustrate the need to manage salinity indices and monitor for Na/CO3 efflorescence</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-0">and irrigation scheduling can moderate hydraulic trade-offs between sands and clays</cite>.
- Clays (Vertisols/Ferralsols/Ultisols in alkaline regions): Peak improvements in structure, nutrient sorption, and crop response often occur around 2% w/w, but benefits are contingent on feedstock and irrigation. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">About 2% was optimal in Vertisols and Ferralsols, while rates >0.25–0.3% raised pH above 7 and reduced TOC, available P, and NH4+—indicating early immobilization/alkalinity stress before higher-dose benefits emerge</cite>. Under wastewater irrigation, higher rates (e.g., ≥5–10% w/w) can further elevate EC and nutrient adsorption, which may be counterproductive for salinity-sensitive crops. <cite id="b68d0bac-2">Higher biochar rates increased EC and nutrient pools under wastewater irrigation, reflecting strong cation/anion release and adsorption</cite>. Meta-analyses suggest that on alkaline clays, benefits plateau and diminishing returns set in; >10 Mg ha−1 is generally useful only for P availability when pH<7.5, and biochar should be applied at lower, potentially one-time doses to avoid repeated immobilization/alkalinity cycles. <cite id="64948a1f-4">Strongly acidic/coarse soils benefit more; >10 Mg ha−1 increases P availability in pH<7.5 but has little influence in alkaline soils; high rates are a “once-in-a-lifetime” practice with long-term benefits accruing from structure and water retention</cite>.

Mechanisms driving decline beyond the peak
Two soil-specific mechanisms commonly cap improvements: nutrient immobilization in the early years (sandy and clay) and alkalinity/sealing constraints in clays. <cite id="64948a1f-2">Moderate biochar dose increases (2–5%) are associated with peak nutrient availability, with higher doses risking nutrient immobilization</cite>. In sands, immobilization is tied to biochar’s high C:N and microbial “mining,” while irrigation-driven flushing can either mitigate immobilization by leaching NH4+ or exacerbate alkalinity/efflorescence from Ca and bicarbonate release on subsequent dry spells. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Higher biochar doses increased pH and EC via carbonate and cation release and promoted Na/CO3 efflorescence risk under irrigation stoppages or low leaching</cite>. In clays, immobilization can be followed by nutrient re-release as biochar degrades and as leaching increases through irrigation, but the same ash-driven pH rise can precipitate Ca–P and Ca–CO3 at the surface and within aggregates, reducing NH4+ availability and potentially damaging crusting and macroporosity. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">In Ferralsols, rates above 0.25% raised pH beyond 7 with decreases in TOC, available P, and NH4+, while 2% biochar later increased NO3− and biomass, indicating a transition from immobilization/alkalinity stress to recovery with higher dose</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-0">and clays are more prone to packing and reduced macroporosity under higher biochar volumes</cite>.

Feedstock, irrigation regime, and monitoring
Optimal rates are highly feedstock- and system-dependent. Wood-derived biochars with lower ash/lime content can be applied at higher rates on alkaline clays without immediate alkalinity overshoot, whereas palm oil waste or agricultural residues with higher ash/lime can push pH above 7 at ~1–2% and cause early nutrient declines. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">In Red Ferralsols, higher pH and lower TOC/P/NH4+ occurred at 0.25–0.3% dose, with 2% ultimately improving yield and NO3−, emphasizing soil- and feedstock-specific optima</cite>. Under drip irrigation with strong leaching, sandy fields can tolerate up to ~3–5% w/w of low-lime biochar for long-term water/CEC gains but require monitoring of EC, pH, and early-season nutrient status for immobilization; on clays, favor 1–2% for most crops, with spot higher-dose applications to cracking-prone zones under sprinkler/flood systems, and track infiltration and surface alkalinity. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Dose–response EC and pH shifts in sandy soils under irrigation highlight the need to balance nutrient sorption with salinity/alkalinity risks</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-2">and wastewater regimes can magnify EC effects at higher biochar rates</cite>. For alkaline (pH>7.5) fine-textured fields, consider biochar only as a one-off, larger but strategic dose, or choose low-lime biochars and monitor closely for immobilization and efflorescence. <cite id="64948a1f-4">Meta-analysis indicates biochar has little influence on alkaline soils and that high rates should be used sparingly, as long-term benefits accrue from structure and water retention rather than immediate nutrient supply</cite>.

Practical guidance to avoid excess application harms
- Sands under irrigation: Start at ~1–2% w/w (or ~10–20% v/v mixed) for first-year trials; if using alkaline/ashy biochars, favor 1% and monitor EC/pH monthly and for Na/CO3 efflorescence after dry-down; adjust subsequent doses down if immobilization (low soil NO3−, NH4+ spikes early, then P/K reductions) or surface alkalinity appears. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">In coastal saline sands, 1% biochar reduced Na and salt stress, while 2% did not further reduce salinity; pH and EC rose with dose</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-1">and ~10% v/v improved WHC but >10% reduced root depth in turfgrass</cite>.
- Clays under irrigation: Begin at ~1–2% w/w; in Ferralsols/Vertisols, test strips at ~2% may yield earlier improvements in NO3− and biomass than in soils prone to pH overshoot at low rates; avoid >5% w/w on alkaline clays without monitoring; in wastewater systems, cap higher rates due to EC/salinity risk. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">About 2% was optimal in Vertisols/Ferralsols; >0.25–0.3% raised pH beyond 7 and reduced TOC, P, and NH4+, with recovery at 2% for some properties</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-2">and higher rates increased EC and nutrient adsorption under wastewater irrigation</cite>.
- Cross-cutting: Use low-lime/low-ash wood biochars on alkaline soils; blend biochar with compost to buffer pH and supply labile C to prevent sharp immobilization; maintain drip leaching fractions ≥10–20% to mitigate surface alkalinity and flush immobilized N; measure WHC, infiltration, EC, pH, and extractable P/K/NH4+ each season. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Biochar-induced pH and EC increases and efflorescence tendencies can be managed via irrigation fractions and dose selection</cite> <cite id="64948a1f-4">meta-analysis underscores feedstock/soil dependence and recommends high-rate strategic application</cite>.

Evidence gaps and how to close them
Literature shows non-monotonic responses, but the exact peak and tipping points vary by climate, irrigation fraction, biochar feedstock, and crop; field lysimeter and strip trials that track leachate EC/pH, soil gas CO2, and nutrient dynamics across 0–5–10–20% rates will refine thresholds. <cite id="fde4ec35-1">A case study found 10% v/v optimal for rooting in sands, with >10% causing anaerobiosis</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-3">while 2% was optimal in some clays, with early pH overshoot at 0.25–0.3%</cite>. Monitoring salinity indices and early nutrient immobilization can move systems from “beneficial sorbent” to “alkalinity/immobilization trap.” <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Dose-dependent increases in EC and pH and associated efflorescence risk in sandy soils under irrigation</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-3">and nutrient depletion at low doses in Ferralsols/Vertisols point to the need for dose-agnostic, real-time management</cite>.

Bottom line
- Sands under irrigation: Peak improvements in water/nutrient retention and crop response generally occur at ~1–2% w/w biochar; higher “volume” rates around 10% v/v can improve rooting but risk waterlogging and nutrient immobilization, with alkaline biochars pushing surface pH/EC and efflorescence at ≤2–3% if leaching is limited. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">1% biochar mitigated salinity, while 2% showed diminishing salinity benefit and rising pH/EC</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-1">~10% v/v improved WHC but >10% reduced root depth in turfgrass</cite> <cite id="64948a1f-2">2–5% rates often peak nutrient availability before immobilization risk</cite>.
- Clays under irrigation: Peak improvements often appear near ~2% w/w, but alkalinity/immobilization can first depress TOC, available P, and NH4+ at 0.25–0.3% and then recover with higher dose; on alkaline clays and under high-EC irrigation, favor ≤1–2% and manage irrigation to avoid surface sealing and salinity stress. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">~2% optimal in Vertisols/Ferralsols; >0.25–0.3% raised pH beyond 7 and decreased TOC, P, and NH4+</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-2">higher rates increased EC and nutrient pools under wastewater irrigation</cite> <cite id="64948a1f-4">>10 Mg ha−1 benefits P only at pH<7.5 and is best as a strategic, lower-frequency dose</cite>.

It may be added to soils to improve soil quality because of the C fundamental role in chemical, biological and physical processes, while also reducing atmospheric CO 2 emissions (Glaser et al., 2002;Lehmann, 2007;Laird, 2008). Title: The 3R Principles for Applying Biochar to Improve Soil Health
Snippet: Soil texture, pH, EC, OC content, available nutrient level, and other properties influence the beneficial effects that could be attained through biochar amendment. Meta-analysis of the reported biochar studies illustrates that strongly acidic (e.g., pH <5.5), coarse-textured soils generally respond more in improved overall health and crop productivity to biochar amendment than neutral or alkaline, fine-textured soils [35,67]. For instance, application of biochar at >10 Mg ha −1 was able to enhance the P availability of pH <7.5 agricultural soils but had little influence on that of alkaline (pH>7.5) soils [89]. Therefore, the type of soil should be examined upon biochar amendment. To maximize its benefits, biochar should be applied to acidic (i.e., pH <6.5), strongly leached soils with low OC contents (e.g., <10 g OC kg −1 soil or organic matter content <2%) [6]. To alkaline soils (e.g., pH >7.5), biochar amendment may not be appropriate. If practiced, wood-derived biochars (relatively low in mineral ash content and lime equivalence) should be considered over other sources of biochars. 

High-quality biochars are rather recalcitrant in the natural environment and can remain in soil over hundreds of years [4]. The short-term benefits (e.g., acid neutralization and nutrient supply) of biochar amendment may dissipate in one or several growing seasons, but the long-term benefits (e.g., improved water and nutrient retention and soil aggregation) will everlastingly persist. At sufficiently high rates, biochar amendment should be a "once-a-life" practice; applying biochar to each crop is clearly not necessary [86]. Consecutive biochar applications may be implemented to bring the cumulative amendment rates to the optimal levels if single applications were carried out at lower rates. 

Thorough mixing with soil is the most efficient method for applying biochar to improve the overall soil health. This method has been extensively used in research and field trials.
</snippet></tool_output>

[54] on sandy soil biochar inclusion demonstrated specific surface area and soil CEC increases relative to untreated soil, since the ability of biochar to adsorb or transport nutrients is a crucial factor for nutrients to be generally retained in soils [5,8,34]. Since biochar has a higher surface area, greater negative surface charge, and greater charge density than other soil organic matter, it has the capacity to adsorb cations to a greater extent. Additionally, biochar has been shown to contribute directly to nutrient uptake, thus reducing nutrient leaching or pollutants, thus increasing nutrient use efficiency with higher yield production and therefore a significant correlation between extractable heavy metals and total applied heavy metals is unlikely [16,34,55]. 

In Egypt under arid and semi-arid conditions, due to the alkaline and calcareous nature of desert soils and low precipitation, no increases in heavy metals in the subsoil or groundwater are expected. In addition, the water table is generally deep and the potential for heavy metals to reach the groundwater is low where biochar or organic manure is used. Therefore, if by accident due to flood irrigation the sandy soil moisture increased above saturation, the hypothesis inferred is that the effect of high rates of biochar application to sandy soils would decrease the concentrations of selected heavy metals in groundwater compared to untreated sandy soils.

Summary and framing under irrigation
Biochar commonly improves irrigation-relevant soil functions by increasing porosity and water retention in coarse-textured soils, enhancing cation and nutrient sorption, and modulating pH and electrical conductivity (EC) via its ash and functional groups; however, these same properties can turn disadvantages if applied in excess, triggering nutrient immobilization during early decomposition, surface alkalinity/efflorescence, or waterlogging/anaerobiosis, especially in sands under frequent leaching and in clays where buffering and drainage constraints are different. <cite id="fde4ec35-0">In sandy soils, biochar’s porous structure increases water retention, CEC, and nutrient sorption, reducing leaching and improving nutrient use efficiency</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-3">and irrigation studies report that dose-dependent increases in pH and EC arise from carbonate dissolution and cation release from biochar, with leaching shifting salts deeper and altering infiltration</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-0">By contrast, in fine-textured soils biochar’s fixed pore sizes decrease moisture availability and can raise bulk density, whereas nutrient retention improvements can still reduce nutrient leaching</cite>.

Sandy soils: when peak improvements occur and why
Across irrigated sandy systems, multiple lines of evidence converge on modest to moderate biochar rates delivering peak gains in water retention, infiltration, and nutrient retention, with deterioration when rates are high due to immobilization and/or surface alkalinity. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">In a coastal saline sandy soil, 1% biochar reduced exchangeable sodium (Na) and salt stress relative to untreated controls, while a higher 2% dose did not further reduce salinity under 10 PSU conditions; nutrient pools increased (K up ~35–68%, Ca up to ~0.44%), and pH rose with dose, illustrating that biochar bound K and Ca and raised alkalinity potential</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-1">Under sandy loam in varied irrigation regimes, increasing biochar dose generally increased available P and K, with higher-dose biochar richer in available P particularly beneficial where background P was low</cite>. <cite id="fde4ec35-1">For turfgrass grown on sandy Ultisols, an optimal incorporation near 10% v/v improved water/nutrient retention and root performance, but more than 10% detrimentally affected root depth due to anaerobic conditions from higher water retention</cite>. <cite id="fde4ec35-4">In alkaline, coarse-textured soils, biochar decreased nitrate leaching and increased mineral N at harvest, highlighting that biochar’s chemistry enhances N retention and long-term availability</cite>.

Mechanistically, the “sweet spot” in sands under irrigation reflects a balance between added porosity/CEC (which cut leaching), immediate nutrient immobilization during biochar decomposition (due to C:N), and risk of surface alkalinity and salt efflorescence from Ca and carbonate-bearing feedstocks. <cite id="fde4ec35-0">Biochar adsorbs cations and increases CEC in sandy soils, reducing nutrient leaching</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-3">but higher doses raise pH and EC via dissolution of biochar surface carbonates and cation exchange, creating conditions favorable to Na/CO3 efflorescence and potential phytotoxic alkalinity</cite>. <cite id="64948a1f-2">Synthesis across stress studies indicates yield responses often rise to moderate biochar rates (2–5% by weight) and then level or decline, with higher doses risking nutrient immobilization</cite>.

Practical implication: for sandy soils under irrigation, peak improvements in infiltration, water retention, P/K availability, and yield tend to occur around 1–2% w/w biochar in most settings, with higher “volume” rates near 10% v/v effective for rooting but risking waterlogging above ~10% v/v; exceeding ~2–3% w/w with alkaline/ashy biochars can elevate surface alkalinity and trigger Ca/Na efflorescences, especially under low leaching fractions. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">One coastal sandy study achieved salinity mitigation at 1% biochar and showed diminishing returns at 2% for salinity reduction, while nutrient sorption and pH kept rising with dose</cite> <cite id="fde4ec35-1">and turfgrass work suggests ~10% v/v is a root/WHC tipping point in sandy Ultisols</cite> <cite id="64948a1f-2">with 2–5% often peaking nutrient availability before immobilization risk increases</cite>.

Clay soils: when peak improvements occur and why
In fine-textured/clay soils, biochar also improves aggregation, porosity, and nutrient sorption, but the soil’s inherent drainage constraints and buffering mean problems can arise at higher rates via surface sealing, reduced macroporosity, and alkalinity-driven nutrient lock-up. <cite id="b68d0bac-0">Biochar increases macroaggregation and modifies hydraulic properties; in clays it can reduce available moisture relative to sands due to packing effects</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-2">Under wastewater irrigation (high EC inflows), higher biochar rates more strongly increased EC and nutrients by boosting cation/anion release and adsorption, indicating that nutrient-binding capacity can raise salinity indices for clays</cite>. Critically, dose–response mapping in tropical fine-textured soils shows that while low rates improve fertility, higher rates can overshoot optimal pH and deplete available P/NH4, with some optimal performance at ~2% w/w in Vertisols/Ferralsols before penalties emerge. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">A 2% application rate was optimal in Acrisol, Red Ferralsol, and Vertisol; rates >0.25–0.3% raised pH above 7 in Ferralsols and decreased TOC, available P, and NH4+, whereas 2% restored NO3− and improved maize biomass and root elongation, underscoring strong clay-type dependence</cite>.

Mechanistically, clays peak at higher initial rates before alkalinity and nutrient sorption/immobilization trade-offs dominate because their high buffering power and CEC retain more cations, but biochar’s ash and functional groups can push pH into alkaline ranges, precipitating Ca–Corg complexes and phosphates and reducing NH4+ availability until rainfall/leaching mobilizes residues. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">In Red Ferralsols, rates above 0.25% increased pH beyond 7, with concomitant drops in TOC, available P, and NH4+, while 2% biochar increased NO3− and improved root growth and yield, indicating a non-monotonic response where early immobilization occurs before later nutrient release and structure benefits dominate</cite>. <cite id="b68d0bac-2">Higher rates under wastewater irrigation further raise EC and nutrient adsorption/desorption, which can stress salinity-sensitive crops on clays</cite>. Meta-analyses also caution that alkaline/fine-textured soils benefit less from biochar, and high rates are best reserved for single, strategic applications to reach thresholds, rather than repeated annual dosing. <cite id="64948a1f-4">Meta-analyses show strongly acidic, coarse-textured soils respond more than neutral/alkaline, fine-textured soils; biochar at >10 Mg ha−1 enhances P availability in pH<7.5 soils but has little effect in alkaline soils, supporting a one-off or lower-frequency dosing strategy</cite>.

Putting numbers together: peak ranges and transition to harm under irrigation
- Sands (Ultisols/coastal/plains): A pragmatic dose–response pattern under irrigation shows improvements in WHC, infiltration, P/K availability, and yield peak at roughly 1–2% biochar (w/w), with evidence of diminishing or reversing returns when exceeding ~2–3% w/w—especially for alkaline/ashy biochars where surface alkalinity and efflorescence risk rise. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">In coastal saline sands, 1% biochar lowered Na and salt stress, while 2% did not further reduce salinity; pH and EC rose with dose due to carbonate/cation release</cite>. <cite id="fde4ec35-1">For turfgrass, about 10% v/v improved WHC and rooting, but >10% v/v reduced root depth by promoting anaerobiosis</cite>. <cite id="64948a1f-2">Across stress conditions, moderate rates of 2–5% by weight commonly peak nutrient availability and yield before immobilization sets in</cite>. Under sprinkler/flood irrigation with low leaching fractions, holding to ≤1–2% w/w of wood-derived, lower-lime biochar is safer to avoid alkalinity and nutrient lock-up; sands with good leaching (e.g., drip with 10–30% leaching fractions) can tolerate up to ~3–5% w/w for structural/CEC benefits if monitored for EC/P availability and early nutrient immobilization. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Dose-dependent EC and pH shifts illustrate the need to manage salinity indices and monitor for Na/CO3 efflorescence</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-0">and irrigation scheduling can moderate hydraulic trade-offs between sands and clays</cite>.
- Clays (Vertisols/Ferralsols/Ultisols in alkaline regions): Peak improvements in structure, nutrient sorption, and crop response often occur around 2% w/w, but benefits are contingent on feedstock and irrigation. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">About 2% was optimal in Vertisols and Ferralsols, while rates >0.25–0.3% raised pH above 7 and reduced TOC, available P, and NH4+—indicating early immobilization/alkalinity stress before higher-dose benefits emerge</cite>. Under wastewater irrigation, higher rates (e.g., ≥5–10% w/w) can further elevate EC and nutrient adsorption, which may be counterproductive for salinity-sensitive crops. <cite id="b68d0bac-2">Higher biochar rates increased EC and nutrient pools under wastewater irrigation, reflecting strong cation/anion release and adsorption</cite>. Meta-analyses suggest that on alkaline clays, benefits plateau and diminishing returns set in; >10 Mg ha−1 is generally useful only for P availability when pH<7.5, and biochar should be applied at lower, potentially one-time doses to avoid repeated immobilization/alkalinity cycles. <cite id="64948a1f-4">Strongly acidic/coarse soils benefit more; >10 Mg ha−1 increases P availability in pH<7.5 but has little influence in alkaline soils; high rates are a “once-in-a-lifetime” practice with long-term benefits accruing from structure and water retention</cite>.

Mechanisms driving decline beyond the peak
Two soil-specific mechanisms commonly cap improvements: nutrient immobilization in the early years (sandy and clay) and alkalinity/sealing constraints in clays. <cite id="64948a1f-2">Moderate biochar dose increases (2–5%) are associated with peak nutrient availability, with higher doses risking nutrient immobilization</cite>. In sands, immobilization is tied to biochar’s high C:N and microbial “mining,” while irrigation-driven flushing can either mitigate immobilization by leaching NH4+ or exacerbate alkalinity/efflorescence from Ca and bicarbonate release on subsequent dry spells. <cite id="fde4ec35-3">Higher biochar doses increased pH and EC via carbonate and cation release and promoted Na/CO3 efflorescence risk under irrigation stoppages or low leaching</cite>. In clays, immobilization can be followed by nutrient re-release as biochar degrades and as leaching increases through irrigation, but the same ash-driven pH rise can precipitate Ca–P and Ca–CO3 at the surface and within aggregates, reducing NH4+ availability and potentially damaging crusting and macroporosity. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">In Ferralsols, rates above 0.25% raised pH beyond 7 with decreases in TOC, available P, and NH4+, while 2% biochar later increased NO3− and biomass, indicating a transition from immobilization/alkalinity stress to recovery with higher dose</cite> <cite id="b68d0bac-0">and clays are more prone to packing and reduced macroporosity under higher biochar volumes</cite>.

Feedstock, irrigation regime, and monitoring
Optimal rates are highly feedstock- and system-dependent. Wood-derived biochars with lower ash/lime content can be applied at higher rates on alkaline clays without immediate alkalinity overshoot, whereas palm oil waste or agricultural residues with higher ash/lime can push pH above 7 at ~1–2% and cause early nutrient declines. <cite id="b68d0bac-3">In Red Ferralsols, higher pH and lower TOC/P/NH4+ occurred at 0.25–0.3% dose, with 2% ultimately improving yield and NO3−, emphasizing soil- and feedstock-specific optima</cite>. Title: Wheat Crop Yield and Changes in Soil Biological and Heavy Metals Status in a Sandy Soil Amended with Biochar and Irrigated with Drainage Water
Snippet: Biochar is a carbon-rich product, and its potential to improve soil fertility and decrease the bioavailability and leachability of a range of heavy metal contaminants within soils has been recognized globally [4,5]. In particular, sandy soil has a limited specific surface area (0.01-0.1 m 2 g −1 ) compared to clay soil (5-750 m 2 g −1 ), thus their water pollutant or nutrient retention capacities are low [52]. 

The central quality of biochar as a soil conditioner is its highly porous structure, which improves water retention and increases soil surface area [4,49,52,53]. A study by Liang et al. [54] on sandy soil biochar inclusion demonstrated specific surface area and soil CEC increases relative to untreated soil, since the ability of biochar to adsorb or transport nutrients is a crucial factor for nutrients to be generally retained in soils [5,8,34]. Since biochar has a higher surface area, greater negative surface charge, and greater charge density than other soil organic matter, it has the capacity to adsorb cations to a greater extent. Additionally, biochar has been shown to contribute directly to nutrient uptake, thus reducing nutrient leaching or pollutants, thus increasing nutrient use efficiency with higher yield production and therefore a significant correlation between extractable heavy metals and total applied heavy metals is unlikely [16,34,55]. 

In Egypt under arid and semi-arid conditions, due to the alkaline and calcareous nature of desert soils and low precipitation, no increases in heavy metals in the subsoil or groundwater are expected. In addition, the water table is generally deep and the potential for heavy metals to reach the groundwater is low where biochar or organic manure is used. Therefore, if by accident due to flood irrigation the sandy soil moisture increased above saturation, the hypothesis inferred is that the effect of high rates of biochar application to sandy soils would decrease the concentrations of selected heavy metals in groundwater compared to untreated sandy soils.

Title: Biochar improves soil physical characteristics and strengthens root architecture in Muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia L.)
Snippet: Biochar, also named "agrichar, " is a relatively stable carbon compound formed by the thermal decomposition of various biomass materials under low oxygen conditions [1,2]. The use of biochar as amendment can improve water and nutrient retention in soil and stimulate plant growth [3][4][5]. In the southeastern United States, sandy soil is a typical soil type of the "Ultisols. " Its limited water-holding capacity (WHC) led to leaching of water and nutrients [6]. Recently, biochar-related research is increasing rapidly and many benefits of soil amendment on Ultisols soil have been intensively investigated, including enhancing chemical and physical characteristics as well as fertility of soils [7]. Therefore, biochar is considered as one of the potential solutions to improve soil fertility and crop production in sandy soils. 

Most of the work done on biochar amendment focused on plant aboveground growth and yield, but very few on root architecture [8][9][10]. Plant root systems play an important role in plant growth as they are the first contact point between biochar particles and growing plants when absorbing water and nutrients [11]. Thus, biochar application may change root morphology, functioning, and hence affect plant performance. Therefore, it is important to determine how root traits respond to biochar application in sustainable soil management practice [12,13]. 

Biochar can improve root-soil interactions in distinct root-soil zones for increasing root activity [11,14]. Biochar-induced improvement in root growth and development may be associated with at least two mechanisms: (i) enhanced nutrient supply by serving as a direct nutrient source and (ii) helped increase nutrient retention and availability in the rhizosphere and bulk soils [14]. Biochar incorporation rate is highly dependent of crop and soil type. An optimal amount of biochar in sandy soil for turfgrass is close to 10% (v/v) considering root depth and soil WHC. Incorporation of more than 10% biochar in sandy soils may detrimentally affect plant root depth. It may be because of anaerobic conditions which are due to higher soil water retention and less oxygen in pore space [15].

Title: Evaluating biochar’s potential to reduce nitrate leaching and enhance wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) yield under different nitrogen management practices
Snippet: In alkaline sandy loam soils, biochar can be useful as a N-limiting agent, enhancing the retention of N in forms less prone to leaching yet plant-available in the long term. Based on this, biochar application likely improved physicochemical retention, enhancing N retention and minimizing leaching losses 42 . In line with our results, Zhao et al. 43 , Purkaystha et al. 44 found that biochar use in coarse-textured soils led to a decrease in nutrient leaching potential due to enhanced water and nutrient retention capacity. The higher retention of N in pots amended with biochar clearly led to high post-harvest soil MN and higher plant N uptake. The chemistry of biochar, along with its interactions with the soil matrix, has been demonstrated to play a pivotal role in the transformation of applied N into plant-available forms, thereby enhancing N supply and efficiency 44 . Reduced NO 3 -leaching in the mid-to-late growing phase (34-74 days after sowing) was attributed to higher N retention levels due to biochar. These results emphasize the key role of biochar in alleviating NO 3 -leaching and maximizing N cycling in alkaline coarse-textured soils, and the sustainable production of wheat.

Biochar, also named "agrichar, " is a relatively stable carbon compound formed by the thermal decomposition of various biomass materials under low oxygen conditions [1,2]. The use of biochar as amendment can improve water and nutrient retention in soil and stimulate plant growth [3][4][5]. In the southeastern United States, sandy soil is a typical soil type of the "Ultisols. " Its limited water-holding capacity (WHC) led to leaching of water and nutrients [6]. Recently, biochar-related research is increasing rapidly and many benefits of soil amendment on Ultisols soil have been intensively investigated, including enhancing chemical and physical characteristics as well as fertility of soils [7]. Therefore, biochar is considered as one of the potential solutions to improve soil fertility and crop production in sandy soils. 

Most of the work done on biochar amendment focused on plant aboveground growth and yield, but very few on root architecture [8][9][10]. Plant root systems play an important role in plant growth as they are the first contact point between biochar particles and growing plants when absorbing water and nutrients [11]. Thus, biochar application may change root morphology, functioning, and hence affect plant performance. Therefore, it is important to determine how root traits respond to biochar application in sustainable soil management practice [12,13]. 

Biochar can improve root-soil interactions in distinct root-soil zones for increasing root activity [11,14]. Biochar-induced improvement in root growth and development may be associated with at least two mechanisms: (i) enhanced nutrient supply by serving as a direct nutrient source and (ii) helped increase nutrient retention and availability in the rhizosphere and bulk soils [14]. Biochar incorporation rate is highly dependent of crop and soil type. An optimal amount of biochar in sandy soil for turfgrass is close to 10% (v/v) considering root depth and soil WHC. Incorporation of more than 10% biochar in sandy soils may detrimentally affect plant root depth. It may be because of anaerobic conditions which are due to higher soil water retention and less oxygen in pore space [15].

documents.title: Evaluating biochar’s potential to reduce nitrate leaching and enhance wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) yield under different nitrogen management practices
documents.snippet: In alkaline sandy loam soils, biochar can be useful as a N-limiting agent, enhancing the retention of N in forms less prone to leaching yet plant-available in the long term. Based on this, biochar application likely improved physicochemical retention, enhancing N retention and minimizing leaching losses 42 . In line with our results, Zhao et al. 43 , Purkaystha et al. 44 found that biochar use in coarse-textured soils led to a decrease in nutrient leaching potential due to enhanced water and nutrient retention capacity. The higher retention of N in pots amended with biochar clearly led to high post-harvest soil MN and higher plant N uptake. The chemistry of biochar, along with its interactions with the soil matrix, has been demonstrated to play a pivotal role in the transformation of applied N into plant-available forms, thereby enhancing N supply and efficiency 44 . Reduced NO 3 -leaching in the mid-to-late growing phase (34-74 days after sowing) was attributed to higher N retention levels due to biochar. These results emphasize the key role of biochar in alleviating NO 3 -leaching and maximizing N cycling in alkaline coarse-textured soils, and the sustainable production of wheat.

Irrigation scheduling was performed using electronic low-tension tensiometers (Tensioswitch, Tensio-Technik, Germany) that control irrigation based on substrate matric potential. Tensiometers were installed at the midpoint of different pots in order to supply a representative reading of the moisture tension. Tensiometers were connected to an electronic programmer that controlled the beginning (-5 kPa) and the end of irrigation (-1 kPa), which correspond to high and low substrate water potential set points. The leaching fraction of the six substrates after each irrigation varied in a range from 10% (P100) to 30% (BC100) of Biochar is fine-grained and porous charcoal produced after 300-500°C biomass pyrolysis under partial exclusion of oxygen. It may be added to soils to improve soil quality because of the C fundamental role in chemical, biological and physical processes, while also reducing atmospheric CO 2 emissions (Glaser et al., 2002;Lehmann, 2007;Laird, 2008). Soil application of biochar has many environmental advantages over the use of organic manures or compost, it is a porous material with a high inner surface area which helps to retain more water and increase saturated hydraulic conductivity of soils (Asai et al., 2009). Biochar used as soil amendment can increase soil fertility and crop yield (Van Zwieten et al., 2008), also showing high levels of micro-organic activities (Fowles, 2007). It can improve soils physical structure (Chan et al., 2007) and may also modify soil hydraulic properties (Gaskin et al., 2010). Because of the relatively fixed pore sizes, biochar application increases available moisture in sandy soils and decreases moisture availability in clay soils. Biochar has been found to decrease nutrients leaching thus enhancing their availability (Yamato et al., 2006). Furthermore, its cation exchange capacity (CEC) is consistently higher than that of the whole soil (Lehmann et al., 2003;Liang et al., 2006).

Title: Impact of single biochar application on maize growth and water-fertilizer productivity under different irrigation regimes
Snippet: In especial, the enhancement of P availability was critical in improving soil nutrient quality when biochar was amended under different irrigation conditions. It further showed that higher dose of biochar application with high available P content was to the benefit of activation of P in a sandy loam soil with lower available P in the study. In contrast, available P was greater under the W15 regime than under the W35 regime at the same biochar amendment; this difference was especially obvious in the second growing season. The could be mainly related to the cycle of freezing and thawing in the studied region (Sui et al., 2022). Biochar application in the first growing season could hold more soil P in soil by enhancing the stability of soil aggregates and reducing the release of organic matter, so as to reduce the P loss as leaching and runoff during the melting period. Additionally, Biochar can alter the activity of soil microorganisms involved in organic phosphorus hydrolysis and inorganic phosphorus dissolution by releasing phosphatases and low molecular organic acids, thereby increasing phosphorus bioavailability. Our results are partly supported by those of previous reports (Zhang et al., 2013;Blanco-Canqui, 2017). Biochar increased the available K under two irrigation regimes. This is mainly related to the adsorption of K+ by electrostatic attraction on biocharsoil surface (Abbas et al., 2020). In addition, the effect of biochar on soil pH will in turn change the activity of soil microorganisms, and then stimulate the dissolution of soil potassium-containing minerals, thus increasing the content of available K (water-soluble and exchangeable K) in soil (Kangoma et al., 2017). 

The calculated CFI based on these five soil parameters also improved after the addition of biochar (Figure 6). The CFI was generally increased with increasing biochar application rate for each irrigation regime, the trend was accorded with results of Yang et al. (2022).

While, an increase in EC is related to the nutrients availability in soil under wastewater irrigation treatment; for this, EC was increased in response of biochar amendments at higher rate by increasing available nutrients adsorption. As a result, biochar amendments have a more positive influence for an increase in EC under wastewater irrigation than ground water. Increase in total dissolved solids in wastewater increase EC. EC and organic matter was increased in response of wood derived biochar at higher rate of (15 t ha -1 ) than the manure biochar. Higher rate of biochar amendments increases the release of free cation and anions in the soil, which results in an increase in EC (Reeve et al., 2016); biochar have positive influence on EC and organic matter in response of wood biochar at higher rate on EC and organic matter in soil. 

In results of pooled soil samples, higher C under wastewater irrigation favors the indirect increase of organic matter and promote macroaggregates stability in biochar amended soil. Increase in organic matter favors the formation of macroaggregates in response of higher microbial diversity in soil. Title: Immediate Chemical Response and Potential Phytotoxicity of Different Tropical Soils to Empty Oil Palm Fruit Bunch Biochar Application
Snippet: According to Verheijen et al. (2009), biochar can only be safely applied up to a certain limit, beyond which other soil functions may be compromised. Results showed that the highest application rate of 2.0% was optimal for Acrisol, Red Ferralsol and Vertisol soils, with scores of 0.83, 74 and 0.84, respectively. In the Red Ferralsol, applications higher than 0.25% raised the pH beyond the 7 (optimum range) and decreased TOC, available P, and NH 4 + content, but biochar rate at 2% increased the NO 3 ̶ content and enhanced root elongation after 1 DAI and maize biomass yield. In the Brown Ferralsol, rates above 1% improved soil chemical properties and nutrient uptake but reduced germination and root elongation. These findings support Gul and Whalen's (2016) assertion that soil properties such as clay type, carbon content, and CEC influence biochar's ameliorative effects. The study suggests that the optimal EFB biochar application rate varies across tropical soils, necessitating caution when using it as a soil conditioner.

Title: The 3R Principles for Applying Biochar to Improve Soil Health
Snippet: Soil texture, pH, EC, OC content, available nutrient level, and other properties influence the beneficial effects that could be attained through biochar amendment. Meta-analysis of the reported biochar studies illustrates that strongly acidic (e.g., pH <5.5), coarse-textured soils generally respond more in improved overall health and crop productivity to biochar amendment than neutral or alkaline, fine-textured soils [35,67]. For instance, application of biochar at >10 Mg ha −1 was able to enhance the P availability of pH <7.5 agricultural soils but had little influence on that of alkaline (pH>7.5) soils [89]. Therefore, the type of soil should be examined upon biochar amendment. To maximize its benefits, biochar should be applied to acidic (i.e., pH <6.5), strongly leached soils with low OC contents (e.g., <10 g OC kg −1 soil or organic matter content <2%) [6]. To alkaline soils (e.g., pH >7.5), biochar amendment may not be appropriate. If practiced, wood-derived biochars (relatively low in mineral ash content and lime equivalence) should be considered over other sources of biochars. 

High-quality biochars are rather recalcitrant in the natural environment and can remain in soil over hundreds of years [4]. The short-term benefits (e.g., acid neutralization and nutrient supply) of biochar amendment may dissipate in one or several growing seasons, but the long-term benefits (e.g., improved water and nutrient retention and soil aggregation) will everlastingly persist. At sufficiently high rates, biochar amendment should be a "once-a-life" practice; applying biochar to each crop is clearly not necessary [86]. Consecutive biochar applications may be implemented to bring the cumulative amendment rates to the optimal levels if single applications were carried out at lower rates. 

Thorough mixing with soil is the most efficient method for applying biochar to improve the overall soil health. This method has been extensively used in research and field trials.

In results of pooled soil samples, higher C under wastewater irrigation favors the indirect increase of organic matter and promote macroaggregates stability in biochar amended soil. Increase in organic matter favors the formation of macroaggregates in response of higher microbial diversity in soil. documents.title: Immediate Chemical Response and Potential Phytotoxicity of Different Tropical Soils to Empty Oil Palm Fruit Bunch Biochar Application
documents.snippet: According to Verheijen et al. (2009), biochar can only be safely applied up to a certain limit, beyond which other soil functions may be compromised. Results showed that the highest application rate of 2.0% was optimal for Acrisol, Red Ferralsol and Vertisol soils, with scores of 0.83, 74 and 0.84, respectively. In the Red Ferralsol, applications higher than 0.25% raised the pH beyond the 7 (optimum range) and decreased TOC, available P, and NH 4 + content, but biochar rate at 2% increased the NO 3 ̶ content and enhanced root elongation after 1 DAI and maize biomass yield. In the Brown Ferralsol, rates above 1% improved soil chemical properties and nutrient uptake but reduced germination and root elongation. These findings support Gul and Whalen's (2016) assertion that soil properties such as clay type, carbon content, and CEC influence biochar's ameliorative effects. The study suggests that the optimal EFB biochar application rate varies across tropical soils, necessitating caution when using it as a soil conditioner.

documents.title: The 3R Principles for Applying Biochar to Improve Soil Health
documents.snippet:
Soil texture, pH, EC, OC content, available nutrient level, and other properties influence the beneficial effects that could be attained through biochar amendment. Meta-analysis of the reported biochar studies illustrates that strongly acidic (e.g., pH <5.5), coarse-textured soils generally respond more in improved overall health and crop productivity to biochar amendment than neutral or alkaline, fine-textured soils [35,67]. For instance, application of biochar at >10 Mg ha −1 was able to enhance the P availability of pH <7.5 agricultural soils but had little influence on that of alkaline (pH>7.5) soils [89]. Therefore, the type of soil should be examined upon biochar amendment. To maximize its benefits, biochar should be applied to acidic (i.e., pH <6.5), strongly leached soils with low OC contents (e.g., <10 g OC kg −1 soil or organic matter content <2%) [6]. To alkaline soils (e.g., pH >7.5), biochar amendment may not be appropriate. If practiced, wood-derived biochars (relatively low in mineral ash content and lime equivalence) should be considered over other sources of biochars. 

High-quality biochars are rather recalcitrant in the natural environment and can remain in soil over hundreds of years [4]. The short-term benefits (e.g., acid neutralization and nutrient supply) of biochar amendment may dissipate in one or several growing seasons, but the long-term benefits (e.g., improved water and nutrient retention and soil aggregation) will everlastingly persist. At sufficiently high rates, biochar amendment should be a "once-a-life" practice; applying biochar to each crop is clearly not necessary [86]. Consecutive biochar applications may be implemented to bring the cumulative amendment rates to the optimal levels if single applications were carried out at lower rates. 

Thorough mixing with soil is the most efficient method for applying biochar to improve the overall soil health. This method has been extensively used in research and field trials.

Title: Wheat Crop Yield and Changes in Soil Biological and Heavy Metals Status in a Sandy Soil Amended with Biochar and Irrigated with Drainage Water
Snippet: Biochar is a carbon-rich product, and its potential to improve soil fertility and decrease the bioavailability and leachability of a range of heavy metal contaminants within soils has been recognized globally [4,5]. In particular, sandy soil has a limited specific surface area (0.01-0.1 m 2 g −1 ) compared to clay soil (5-750 m 2 g −1 ), thus their water pollutant or nutrient retention capacities are low [52]. 

The central quality of biochar as a soil conditioner is its highly porous structure, which improves water retention and increases soil surface area [4,49,52,53]. A study by Liang et al. [54] on sandy soil biochar inclusion demonstrated specific surface area and soil CEC increases relative to untreated soil, since the ability of biochar to adsorb or transport nutrients is a crucial factor for nutrients to be generally retained in soils [5,8,34]. Since biochar has a higher surface area, greater negative surface charge, and greater charge density than other soil organic matter, it has the capacity to adsorb cations to a greater extent. Additionally, biochar has been shown to contribute directly to nutrient uptake, thus reducing nutrient leaching or pollutants, thus increasing nutrient use efficiency with higher yield production and therefore a significant correlation between extractable heavy metals and total applied heavy metals is unlikely [16,34,55]. 

In Egypt under arid and semi-arid conditions, due to the alkaline and calcareous nature of desert soils and low precipitation, no increases in heavy metals in the subsoil or groundwater are expected. In addition, the water table is generally deep and the potential for heavy metals to reach the groundwater is low where biochar or organic manure is used. Therefore, if by accident due to flood irrigation the sandy soil moisture increased above saturation, the hypothesis inferred is that the effect of high rates of biochar application to sandy soils would decrease the concentrations of selected heavy metals in groundwater compared to untreated sandy soils.

Snippet: The most positive results are related to biochar application to acidic soils (14% yield increase), neutral pH soils (13%), coarse soils (10%) and medium textured soils (13%) [Jeffery et al. 2011]. It is a livelihood source for approximately 5 million people in the region.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer satisfies both requirements of the verification criterion. (1) It specifies quantitative reversal thresholds: for sandy soils, it states that exceeding ~2-3% w/w causes surface alkalinity and efflorescence risk, and >10% v/v causes anaerobiosis reducing root depth [2,5]; for clay soils, it states that rates >0.25-0.3% raise pH above 7 and decrease TOC, available P, and NH4+ in Ferralsols [9]. (2) It identifies texture-specific differences and explains them mechanistically: sandy soils peak at 1-2% w/w due to lower buffering capacity and higher leaching risk (alkalinity/efflorescence concerns dominate), while clays can tolerate up to ~2% w/w before alkalinity stress due to higher buffering capacity but face earlier pH overshoot at 0.25-0.3% in some soil types; the answer explains these differences are driven by contrasting CEC, buffering power, drainage constraints, and hydraulic properties between the two textures.
other_issues: The answer is extremely verbose and repetitive, with the same points about sandy soils peaking at 1-2% w/w and clay soils at ~2% w/w repeated across multiple sections, reducing clarity and efficiency.

Some citation support is weak or tangential: Reference [7] discusses barley under salinity/drought stress and mentions 2-5% rates in passing but doesn't provide direct evidence for the specific thresholds claimed for sandy vs. clay soils under irrigation.

The '10% v/v' threshold for sandy soils causing anaerobiosis [5] is cited from a turfgrass study on Ultisols, which may not generalize well to other sandy soil contexts under irrigation, though the answer does acknowledge soil-type dependence.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Biochar improves overall soil functionality under irrigation in fine‑textured soils by coupling strong microporous water retention with increased macroporous connectivity that promotes infiltration and drainage; together, these effects reduce chronic saturation while maintaining plant-available water and aeration, especially when biochar is applied at moderate rates and matched to soil and irrigation conditions. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Biochar’s mixed pore system increases macroporosity and aggregate structure (improving infiltration and drainage) while its microporosity raises field capacity, enabling “both ends of the soil water balance” to improve—storing more water while permitting percolation of excess moisture</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Dose matters: moderate rates (∼2–5 wt% in sandy/silty soils) sharply improve water retention without causing chronic wetness, whereas >~10 wt% can plateau water-holding capacity and increase variability, risking saturation</cite>.

How biochar improves water retention and hydraulics without “suffocating” the soil
Fine-textured soils are prone to waterlogging because small pores retain water tightly and drain slowly; biochar introduces hierarchical porosity that physically reorganizes aggregates and creates continuous macropores for rapid water movement. <cite id="d05383d6-2">Across studies, biochar commonly reduces bulk density by 3–31%, increases porosity by 14–64%, and improves wet aggregate stability, which together raise water availability and hydraulic conductivity in ways that depend on soil texture and biochar properties</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-0">In a dose–response NMR analysis, biochar increased macroporosity and aggregate structure, raising infiltration and drainage despite high water retention at elevated biochar fractions; mixed particle sizes and internal porosity avoided clogging and maintained percolation, demonstrating simultaneous gains in field capacity and hydraulic conductivity</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-2">However, direction of hydraulic conductivity change can reverse with texture: some studies report decreases in coarse-textured soils and increases in fine-textured soils, highlighting strong interactions between biochar and native soil hydraulic pathways</cite>.

Aeration and oxygen diffusion during irrigation events
Enhanced water retention can degrade aeration if infiltration is poor or soils are compacted; biochar mitigates this by maintaining air-filled macropores and facilitating oxygen transport into wetted zones. <cite id="743a00d3-0">In column experiments, heavy irrigation induced strong hypoxia in straw-amended soil due to high microbial oxygen demand and low oxygen diffusion, whereas non-amended, compost, and biochar soils remained largely oxic; oxygen remained higher near raw biochar particles likely due to enhanced oxygen diffusion through the char’s porosity</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-1">Moisture and biochar properties modulate gas diffusion: 50–70% WHC is optimal for gas diffusion; water held in biochar pores can reduce gas uptake, and high biochar water occupancy or unsuitable pore wetting can create anoxic microhabitats, underscoring the need to manage moisture and biochar hydrophobicity</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-0">In a related study, biochar soils showed slightly stronger hypoxia than non-amended soil when biochar carried biological loads, indicating that organic coatings may host respiring microorganisms and locally reduce oxygen; raw vs. biofunctionalized biochar therefore differentially affects oxygen diffusion</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-2">At the rhizosphere scale, oxygen is lower and CO2 higher near roots, but biochar-amended soils show greater macro-aggregation and porosity around roots, consistent with improved structure and aeration at the root interface</cite>.

Fine-tuning for irrigation: infiltration, runoff/erosion, and crusting
Irrigation in fine-textured soils often triggers seal formation, reduced infiltration, and runoff; biochar’s physical and chemical properties counter these processes. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Fine particles can clog pores and reduce infiltration in clays, but biochar’s mixed particle sizes and internal porosity avoided clogging and improved both infiltration and field capacity in a clay, highlighting the distinctive balance of macro- and micro-pores</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-2">Meta-analyses and lab studies show biochar reduces bulk density, increases porosity and aggregate stability, and improves permeability; these structural changes increase infiltration and reduce runoff and erosion risks under irrigation</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-0">In practice, maintaining adequate macroporosity improves drainage after irrigation, reducing surface crusting and ponding that otherwise depress oxygen diffusion into surface layers</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-3">In fine sand amended with 3% biochar, total porosity did not change markedly, but water retained at 0 kPa increased significantly, and higher rates (up to 10%) correlated with improved water retention; these results illustrate that even modest biochar additions can buffer dry spells while preserving infiltration capacity</cite>.

Mitigating salinized/alkaline conditions common under irrigation
In many irrigated landscapes, especially arid zones, quality of water and soil can degrade to high salinity and sodicity; biochar improves soil functionality by restoring structure and ion balance. <cite id="12f14005-0">In a two-season field trial in saline–sodic Al‑Ahsa soils, date‑palm biochar at 10–20 t/ha reduced salinity and sodicity, improved infiltration, increased organic carbon and yields, and lowered irrigation demand</cite>. <cite id="12f14005-1">Under saline water irrigation, 10–20 t/ha straw biochar lowered bulk density, raised permeability, and increased mineral N, available P, and K in the topsoil; it also mitigated sodicity, improving wheat leaf area and photosynthesis and increasing grain yield</cite>. <cite id="12f14005-2">Biochar reduced soil SAR via providing Ca2+/Mg2+ and increased CEC to adsorb Na+, displacing Na+ and facilitating its leaching; despite these gains, biochar-amended plots still showed higher EC than controls due to mineral inputs, emphasizing that salt leaching remains necessary under saline irrigation</cite>. <cite id="12f14005-3">Mechanistically, biochar’s porous structure, high surface area, and ion exchange capacity improve soil structure, porosity, water-holding, permeability, and aeration, while reducing Na+ uptake and oxidative stress in plants under salt stress; these properties collectively facilitate wheat production under saline-irrigated conditions</cite>.

Broader soil functionality: aggregation, nutrient cycling, and the rhizosphere
Beyond water and aeration, biochar strengthens soil function by stabilizing aggregates, buffering pH, and hosting microbial communities that support nutrient cycling. <cite id="d05383d6-2">Biochar commonly increases wet aggregate stability by wide margins, with reported improvements from 3% to 226%, reinforcing pore networks and resistance to slaking and dispersion that otherwise degrade infiltration and aeration under irrigation</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Moderate biochar additions sharply improve water retention in sandy or silty soils and can increase infiltration in clays without causing chronic wetness; texture-specific optimal doses help avoid saturation problems</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-1">Poultry-litter biochar doubled water holding in a sandy loam in a greenhouse study; increased macroporosity reduces soil strength and bulk density, enhances permeability, and adsorbs nutrients, cutting leaching while maintaining a steady water supply during drought</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-2">Oxidized biochar at 250 °C increased water retention in sandy soil; production temperature and surface chemistry tune hydrophobicity and nutrient retention, which in turn govern leaching and retention</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-2">Pyrolysis temperature and post-treatments strongly shape internal porosity and surface chemistry, explaining why biochar effects on water retention and hydraulic conductivity vary by feedstock and processing</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-3">A meta-analysis finds “available water” increases by ~30% in coarse soils, ~21% in medium, and ~12% in fine soils, with texture, dose, and particle size as key moderators</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-2">Biochar’s buffering capacity raises pH in acid soils, improving nutrient availability; in the rhizosphere, improved porosity and macro-aggregation enhance oxygen diffusion into root zones, supporting respiration and microbial processes that supply nutrients</cite>.

Practical irrigation outcomes
Field and horticultural systems show that biochar’s improved storage and drainage reduce irrigation frequency and volume while sustaining yields. <cite id="d05383d6-0">A practical guideline to avoid chronic wetness is to not exceed ~10 wt% biochar in most cases (∼100 t/ha in the top 5 cm), with fine-textured soils attaining hydrological ceilings sooner and requiring lower rates to achieve equivalent gains</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-4">In a two‑year irrigated dwarf coconut orchard, biochar doses reduced annual irrigation water demand per plant; the highest retention (40 g/kg soil) lowered irrigation to 20 L plant−1 day−1 on average, illustrating dose‑dependent water savings under frequent irrigation</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-3">In coarser sands, modest 3% biochar significantly raised water content at 0 kPa, and higher rates up to 10% correlated with greater retention; this suggests irrigation scheduling can target deeper infiltration into macropores created by biochar</cite>.

Moderators, risks, and best practices
- Feedstock and processing: <cite id="743a00d3-3">Biochar properties span a wide range depending on feedstock and pyrolysis conditions; low H/C and O/C (e.g., H/C < 0.7, O/C < 0.4) indicate more recalcitrant chars that are often less inhibitory and more stabilizing for long-term soil function</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-1">Hydrophobicity and moisture occupancy of biochar pores alter gas diffusion; testing biochars at 60–100% WHC is recommended to avoid anoxic microhabitats</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-2">Oxidized biochars can increase water retention in sands; temperature and functionalization alter nutrient adsorption and gas-phase interactions</cite>.
- Texture and dose: <cite id="d05383d6-0">Fine-textured soils benefit from biochar’s macroporosity but reach hydrologic capacity quickly; moderate rates (∼2–5 wt%) are often sufficient, with diminishing returns above ~10 wt% and potential variability</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-2">Fine-textured soils may show increased hydraulic conductivity with biochar, whereas coarse-textured soils may see decreases, requiring site-specific calibration</cite>.
- Moisture and timing: <cite id="743a00d3-1">Between 50–70% WHC is optimal for gas diffusion; irrigation that temporarily floods soils reduces diffusion; managing drainage paths and avoiding prolonged ponding preserves oxygen transfer</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Biochar’s “sweet spot” is to maximize field capacity and plant-available water without chronic saturation; structuring infiltration before/after irrigation (e.g., surface crusting control, timely drainage) is critical</cite>.
- Saline/alkaline irrigation: <cite id="12f14005-2">Biochar mitigates sodicity via Ca2+/Mg2+ inputs, CEC, and Na+ displacement/leaching, but salinity from saline water still elevates EC; adequate leaching and quality water management remain necessary</cite>.
- Potential downsides: <cite id="d05383d6-0">Very high biochar rates can plateau water-holding capacity and increase variability, risking anaerobic conditions if macropores become water-filled</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-0">Biofunctionalized biochars can host respiring microbes in coatings that locally reduce oxygen, so biological loading and carbon inputs must be balanced with aeration</cite>. <cite id="d05383d6-2">In some cases, biochar additions can initially reduce hydraulic conductivity in coarse soils or increase it in fine soils; matching particle size and dose to texture prevents unintended hydraulic bottlenecks or clogging</cite>.

Putting it together under irrigation in fine-textured soils
Fine-textured soils under irrigation face a classic trade-off: high clay content and organic matter increase water retention but restrict aeration and infiltration. Biochar resolves this by introducing hierarchical, non-clogging pores that: (i) store additional water at field capacity via micropores; (ii) maintain infiltration and drainage through macropores and aggregate bonding; and (iii) preserve oxygen diffusion pathways into wetted zones, limiting irrigation-induced hypoxia and sustaining root respiration and microbial activity. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Biochar can thus simultaneously raise plant-available water and improve drainage, reducing the risk of chronic saturation and associated root damage</cite>. Under saline/alkaline irrigation regimes, biochar’s ion exchange and structural stabilization further restore infiltration and nutrient availability, enabling higher yields with less water. <cite id="12f14005-0">Field evidence shows reductions in salinity and sodicity, improved infiltration, and decreased irrigation demand alongside yield gains</cite>. These physical, chemical, and biological co-benefits translate to practical irrigation management: deeper, less frequent infiltration into biochar-created macropores; earlier drainage paths to avoid surface ponding; and tailored rates and processing to avoid over-saturation or anoxic microhabitats. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Moderate biochar applications (∼2–10 wt%) calibrated to texture and irrigation intensity usually optimize soil water–air balance, with higher doses reserved for severe drought constraints and monitored to prevent saturation</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-1">Finally, aligning irrigation schedules to maintain moisture within optimal gas-diffusion windows (50–70% WHC) and incorporating biochars with appropriate hydrophobicity and functionality minimizes aeration loss while leveraging water retention gains</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Biochar improves soil functionality under irrigation by coupling increased water storage with enhanced infiltration and drainage, which prevents chronic waterlogging in fine-textured soils. <cite id="d05383d6-0">It increases macroporosity and aggregate structure while adding microporosity, raising field capacity and percolation without necessarily worsening aeration</cite>. 
- Aeration is maintained via enhanced oxygen diffusion into aggregates and rhizosphere during irrigation events, although biochar hydrophobicity and high water occupancy can create local anoxia if not managed. <cite id="743a00d3-0">Biochar soils remained oxic during heavy irrigation where straw-amended soils became hypoxic, likely due to biochar-enhanced oxygen diffusion</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-1">Optimal gas diffusion occurs near 50–70% WHC, and biochar pore water can reduce gas uptake; testing moisture regimes and material properties is essential</cite>. 
- Irrigation-specific risks (crusting, sealing, runoff/erosion, salinization/sodicity) are mitigated by biochar’s structure and chemistry, restoring infiltration, reducing bulk density, and displacing sodium for improved hydraulic conductivity and nutrient availability. <cite id="12f14005-2">Biochar lowers SAR via Ca2+/Mg2+ inputs and promotes Na+ leaching, while increasing CEC and permeability</cite>. 
- Moderators include texture, dose (avoid >10 wt% unless needed), feedstock/temperature (choose low H/C, O/C chars; manage hydrophobicity), and irrigation scheduling to prevent ponding and maintain air-filled porosity. <cite id="d05383d6-0">Texture dictates optimal dose; fine soils saturate sooner and benefit from lower rates</cite>. <cite id="743a00d3-3">Material chemistry strongly influences agronomic performance</cite>. 
- Net effect: biochar improves overall soil functionality under irrigation by preventing water-induced aeration loss while enhancing water storage, infiltration, and nutrient buffering—delivering higher yields with reduced irrigation demand in fine-textured soils when biochar is applied and managed appropriately. <cite id="d05383d6-4">In a two‑year irrigated coconut system, biochar increased soil water storage and reduced irrigation by volume</cite>. <cite id="12f14005-1">Under saline water, 10–20 t/ha straw biochar increased wheat grain yields while mitigating infiltration and sodicity problems</cite>.

Title: Comparison of Biochar Derived from Slow Pyrolysis of Banana Peels and Bunch Stalks in Agricultural Soil Amendment
Snippet: Biochar derived from banana peels and stalks shows significant potential as a soil amendment in agriculture. BPB enhances immediate nutrient availability, while BSB excels in moisture retention and long-term carbon storage. Both biochar types improve water retention, especially in coarsetextured soils. Notably, BSB outperformed its peel counterpart in terms of surface area, porosity, cation exchange capacity (CEC), and moisture retention, increasing the soil's water-holding capacity by up to 30%. This effectiveness makes it particularly suitable for sandy soils prone to water and nutrient leaching. Additionally, BSB was more effective at mitigating swell-shrink behaviour in finetextured soils. Its superior characteristics contributed to enhanced soil aggregate stability and reduced fluctuations in soil volume. While amending fine sand with 3% of any biochar type did not significantly increase total porosity, volumetric water content at 0 kPa saw a significant increase (p < 0.001). The results revealed that BS10% retained the most water, with an R² value of 0.7599, followed by BP10% at 0.745, and so on, indicating that higher biochar application rates correlate with improved water retention. The study also highlighted a negative correlation between soil suction and water retention, suggesting that as suction levels increase, the soil's capacity to retain water diminishes. This relationship is crucial for agricultural applications, irrigation planning, and understanding soil hydrology. By utilizing these insights, farmers and land managers can enhance irrigation strategies, improve crop yields, and adapt to evolving environmental conditions.
</snippet>
